💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Not too long ago, making precise angled cuts meant using a simple miterbox—a block with precut 90- and 45-degree slots—and a squat little saw with more teeth than a piranha.
  • Industry observers note that when it comes to angled cuts for trim, framing, or furniture, few tools match a good miter saw.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Not too long ago, making precise angled cuts meant using a simple miterbox—a block with precut 90- and 45-degree slots—and a squat little saw with more teeth than a piranha. Those old-school setups still have their place, especially for ultra-clean trim cuts without tearout, but they’ve largely been replaced by the more powerful and versatile miter saw.

Industry observers note that when it comes to angled cuts for trim, framing, or furniture, few tools match a good miter saw. A circular blade mounted on a hinged, pivoting arm delivers fast, consistent, and precise cuts at a wide range of angles—something handsaws and circular saws can’t replicate as easily.

Recent findings suggest that the best models combine clean cutting power with accurate miter and bevel adjustments, smooth sliding action, and enough stability to stay precise while cutting dense wood. Features like clear cutline indicators, effective dust collection, and easily adjustable fences also make a huge difference when you’re making cuts all day.

Whether you’re building a garden bed or installing window trim, a miter saw is the fastest way to get accurate, repeatable results.

According to recent reports, when selecting potential options for the original version of this article, author Alex Rennie, a former residential and commercial carpenter in Newly introduced York City, first put together a rough collection of options based on brands and saw types he had found to be most useful to him over the years. After paring that list down, he put each saw through a comprehensive series of tests.

Paul Smith updated this article most recently with the Milwaukee M18 FUEL 18V Sliding Compound Miter Saw, which impressed him during testing. He is in the process of testing more models and will update this article with the results of those tests when they are available. In the meantime, those models are included below as recommended miter saws based on reputation, product specs, features, price point, and online customer reviews.

Unlike most sliding saws that use rails to slide the blade forward and backward, this Bosch miter saw uses an axial-arm mechanism that eliminates the need for rear clearance. This unique design (also used by this Bosch model) allows the saw to take up considerably less space on your workbench without compromising overall cut capacity.

We loved the lever locks that secure the arm in place during transport (although we weren’t as much of a fan of the saw’s hefty 65-pound weight), and the smoothness of the arm, combined with the rubber handle grip, made this an especially comfortable saw to operate.

It’s worth noting that while the clear blade guard (compared to the black of the DeWalt models) provides a clearer view of the cutline, this saw lacks a shadow or laser line feature.

Full Bosch GCM12SD Miter Saw Review.

What the Skil 10-inch dual-bevel miter saw lacks in refinement—things like pro-level build quality, multiple bevel detents, and high-end dust collection—it makes up for in capability and cost. At about half the price of most major brands, it delivers consistently clean cuts on a stable, well-constructed turntable.

Recent findings suggest that the motor spins the blade up to 4,800 rpm quickly, so there’s little wait between cuts. In use, cuts were smooth along the rails as I cut through 2x12s, with no tearout or flyaway pieces. The saw is capable of bevels up to 48 degrees left and 45 degrees right—important if you’re making compound miter cuts for things like crown molding. There is a preset detent at 45 degrees left—a common cutting angle—but any bevel angle in between is easily locked down via the rear bevel knob. Even so, it proved accurate across those settings—I had no trouble dialing in compound miters—cuts that employ both miter and bevel cuts—for crown molding that lined up cleanly from both sides.

Ergonomics are a highlight. The trigger sits naturally within the grip, and it’s the only saw I tested that feels equally comfortable left- or right-handed. That might seem minor, but when you’re stretched out on a tricky compound cut, being able to switch hands makes a real difference. Finally, at less than 50 pounds, this saw is no trouble to move around your yard during setup changes or throw in your truck at the end of the day.

Full Skil 10-inch Miter Saw Review.

This dual-bevel, 10-inch saw packs a lot of power and features into one relatively small and comparatively inexpensive package. With nine positive miter stops and a cutting capacity of 12 inches on the bed, you’ll get up to 500 cuts on a single battery charge.

LED line indicators ensure precision, and a bevel pivot that's as easy to access as it is to operate rounds out this saw's top features. While it's not the most powerful saw, even compared to other cordless options, this one holds its own among the arguably bigger names that populate this list in every other way.

Sources indicate that this DeWalt miter saw provides serious power and performance. We found that it maintained speed and power really well during our cut tests, but because it’s cordless, you don’t need to sacrifice mobility when you’re working with it.

The included stabilizer bar ensured that the saw felt sturdy and stable while we cut, and the included LED work light created a convenient, precise shadow line to maximize accuracy. We also appreciated how well the instruction manual walked us through all the different operations, giving us comprehensive instructions on a variety of cuts.

In a recent development, at a little over 50 pounds (without the 20-volt battery, which you’ll have to buy separately) and with a top-mounted carrying handle, this was one of the easier saws to transport during testing. Plus, this saw’s dust port was located on the side, instead of the rear, which made it easier to fit on a smaller workbench.

With dual-bevel capabilities, smooth gliding rails, and user-friendly controls and adjustment knobs, this cordless powerhouse handles everything from 13.5-inch-wide cuts to 6.5-inch-tall baseboards.

Industry observers note that this saw won’t be your go-to if you’re working with large lumber. Nothing bigger than a 2x4 is recommended here, but if that type of work isn’t on your horizon, this saw is as easy to maneuver as it is to operate.

Industry observers note that its small size and extremely accurate blade make it ideal for using indoors to cut trim, flooring, and picture framing. And at just over 14 pounds, it’s a breeze to move from room to room as you work. We also like the gooseneck type of LED built into the blade housing for throwing light on your entire cut. And the 64-tooth blade delivers a clean, precise cut every time.

It has been revealed that if you believe you get what you pay for, this Makita 8-1/2-inch miter saw makes the case. Tools should solve problems—and this one addresses a major one in its category: size versus capability. A 12-inch saw powers through 4x4s but is heavy and space-hungry; a compact 6-inch is portable but limited. This Makita saw lands squarely in between.

This 40-volt cordless saw delivers corded-level power in a lighter package—roughly 10 to 20 pounds less than larger models—while still handling 12-inch crosscuts. Its forward-facing rails save valuable workspace, letting it sit flush against a wall without the usual rear clearance.

Build quality stands out immediately. The heavy aluminum turntable feels rigid under load, with precise detents that lock in smoothly at common angles—no fighting to find your mark. Preset bevel stops on both sides add convenience, and the front-mounted bevel lock means no awkward reaching over the saw.

In a recent development, makita also includes dual dust collection options: a standard bag or a ducted port for a dedicated system. Pair it with Makita’s AWS technology and pulling the trigger wirelessly activates a compatible vacuum—an easy, thoughtful upgrade for shop workflow.

Recent findings suggest that prior to using this saw, I read that some people had issues with the out-of-the-box accuracy of the table in relation to the blade. This situation is problematic when cutting trim, for instance, because it needs to fit perfectly.

In a recent development, I personally experienced none of that. I cut a variety of woods with this saw—from 2x10s to MDF trim—and the results completely satisfied me. Cuts were clean, splinter-free, and above all, accurate at connection.

The saw is powerful, thanks in part to its brushless motor and impressive battery, which Milwaukee claims makes 330 cuts per charge, but I honestly ran out of wood before that number (and according to the battery indicators, I still had half a charge remaining).

According to recent reports, milwaukee puts a lot of effort into getting its shadow line system clear and precise, and I appreciate that when it comes to eyeing up my cuts. As an added bonus, I find the LED field is the best of any saw I’ve used, cordless or otherwise. My only complaints are that the rear bevel is a little clunky to maneuver and the table extenders have an underwhelming feel to them. If you’re expanding your Milwaukee cordless platform, this saw is a great add.

According to recent reports, A few of our readers gave us grief earlier this year for overlooking Evolution’s jobsite table saw on our list of the best table saws, so I called one in. I ran a piece of old angle iron through it before proceeding to cut hardwood, plywood, and pine trim with minimal tearout. My takeaway was that the saw lived up to the hype. Now, I’m curious how Evolution’s 10-inch miter saw handles the same materials.

I’ll start with framing lumber and trim to see how accurately the saw repeats miters and how cleanly it cuts in both bevel directions. Then, I’ll cut some aluminum angle stock and light-gauge steel tubing before moving on to hardwood with the same blade. I want to see how much cleanup each piece of metal needs and whether that last pair of hardwood miters fits together as neatly as the first pair of standard lumber and pine base molding. All throughout, I’ll be looking at standard saw features, as well, including motor power, build quality, table detents, LED lighting or shadow lines, and dust collection.

The three main types of miter saws are compound, dual compound, and sliding. Each variation performs specific functions and cuts better than the others, so it’s notable that you understand their differences and also have a decent idea of how you proposal on using your saw.

In addition to lowering straight down for perpendicular crosscuts, the blade of a compound miter saw also pivots from side to side for angled “miter” cuts, and it tilts to one side for bevel cuts. A “compound” cut utilizes both of these functions in one motion and is commonly used to create things like picture frames or to cut crown molding for installation.

Instead of tilting to only one side for bevel cuts, dual compound saws (also called “double” or “double-bevel” compound saws) tilt in both directions. This makes work much faster than using a standard compound saw because while a compound saw technically makes all the same cuts as a dual compound saw, its single-bevel design means you spend more time flipping workpieces around to cut opposite angles.

These two non-sliding types are solid options for homeowners who want a reasonably compact and portable machine.

A standard compound miter saw drops straight down onto the board. It’s great for narrow stock but limited by the diameter of the blade. A sliding compound miter saw adds rails that let the blade travel forward and backward during the course of the cut. This feature dramatically increases the width of material the saw can handle—making it possible to cut wider boards in a single pass. If you’re cutting a lot of shelving, flooring, or wide trim, a sliding miter saw, such as the DeWalt 20V MAX XR Dual-Bevel Sliding Miter Saw, is usually worth the extra cost and size.

When shopping for a miter saw, you’ll also need to decide what type of power source you prefer.

Recent findings suggest that cordless miter saws have improved dramatically over the last few years, mostly due to the evolution of high-capacity lithium-ion batteries and the inclusion of brushless motors. Today’s 18- and 20-volt models offer plenty of power for trim work and general carpentry without sacrificing the portability that makes cordless power tools appealing in the first place.

In a recent development, I like knowing I can set up the saw anywhere and get to work without worrying about finding power or running an extension cord through an open door or window. That mentioned, corded saws still hold the edge when it comes to cutting ability and run time.

Most miter saws come with 10- or 12-inch blades, and that difference has a big impact on what type of cuts and tasks the saw excels at.

Recent findings suggest that A 10-inch saw, such as the Metabo HPT Single Bevel Compound Miter Saw, is typically lighter and easier to move around your shop or from room to room. It’s more than capable of cutting trim, flooring, and smaller dimensional lumber.

A 12-inch saw, on the other hand, gives you significantly more cutting capacity—especially when you’re working with wider boards or tall trim pieces like crown molding. 12-inch saws, like our Best Overall choice, the Bosch GCM12SD Dual-Bevel Sliding Miter Saw, are a bit more awkward to move around the workplace.

Sources indicate that A large saw also adds bulk and takes up more room in the shop or truck. But the trade-off to those negatives is that you’re far less likely to run into a job that you simply can’t handle. I’d rather deal with the extra footprint than discover upon starting a project that my saw is undersized. If you have the space, it’s often better to size up.

Industry observers note that blade speed, measured in rpm (revolutions per minute), is another important performance indicator. Most miter saws operate between 3,000 and 5,500 rpm, and naturally, higher speeds increase your cutting efficiency. Some saws, like the Hilti Nuron 22V miter saw, even allow you to customize your speed to a specific task, which makes it uniquely versatile.

That said, the relationship between the saw blade diameter and rpm makes comparing the speed of two miter saws a little more complex. Two saws running at the same rpm, but using different-sized blades—let’s say 7¼-inch and 12-inch—will not cut at the same speed. That’s because even though the center of each blade is spinning at the same speed, the outer edge of the 12-inch blade will turn faster than the edge of the 7¼-inch one.

Things get even more complicated when we bring the blade’s tooth count into the mix, with higher-tooth blades reducing speed. As a beginner, you can drive yourself a little crazy trying to determine the perfect combination of blade factors, so I’d recommend relying on your saw’s instruction manual for basic guidance.

Sources indicate that modern miter saws often include features designed to help you cut more accurately and consistently. Some use laser guides to project the cut line, while others use LED systems that cast a shadow from the blade, so you can see exactly where it will land. Detents at common angle stops around the saw table—like 22.5 degrees and 45 degrees—also make it faster to dial in repeated cuts. These features aren’t essential, but they make a noticeable difference when you’re making dozens of cuts in a row.

#157368. Tech Report: What do cadaver dogs smell when they find a buried body?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (971 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What do cadaver dogs smell when they find a buried body?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a pilot study, three cadaver dogs and an electronic nose searched the same grave to see how the dogs’ alerts lined up with the device’s readings.
  • Recent findings suggest that when a cadaver dog lies down over a patch of ground, a search team treats it as the word of an expert.
  • Handlers train the dogs on bone and fluid from decomposing bodies, but the exact chemicals a dog responds to are still unknown.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a pilot study, three cadaver dogs and an electronic nose searched the same grave to see how the dogs’ alerts lined up with the device’s readings.

Recent findings suggest that when a cadaver dog lies down over a patch of ground, a search team treats it as the word of an expert. The expert can’t explain its reasoning, though.

Handlers train the dogs on bone and fluid from decomposing bodies, but the exact chemicals a dog responds to are still unknown.

Over two months, an Australian research team tested three police dogs and a handheld electronic nose at the same grave.

The dogs located the grave consistently after researchers probed the soil, and the electronic nose picked up stronger signals after probing.

The study rests on a single buried donor and three dogs, so the authors call it a pilot.

Amber Brown, now at the University of North Florida, conducted the research while completing her doctorate at the University of Technology Sydney.

Maiken Ueland, who directs the forensic research site where the body was buried, supervised it, with co-authors at the University of Windsor in Canada and in China.

“We don’t know exactly what they are smelling – whether it’s a single compound or a combination of compounds,” Ueland said.

“The electronic nose can provide greater certainty during training by showing whether decomposition odor is present in an area, including when a dog does not alert.”.

Industry observers note that the body belonged to a 79-year-old man who donated it to research. Five days after his death in March 2020, staff buried him about 2 feet (60 centimeters) down in a 12-acre (4.9-hectare) forest plot in western Sydney.

Three empty graves were dug the same day so the dogs couldn’t simply react to disturbed soil.

The grave then sat untouched for 98 days, long enough to match the standard definition of a long-term missing person. Searches ran on six days between July and September.

That is a Sydney winter, with daily averages between 48°F and 57°F (9°C and 14°C), when buried bodies give off less odor.

Industry observers note that on five of the six search days, the team pushed a probe into the grave at 14 points to let trapped gas escape. Soil holds the chemicals of decay the way a sponge holds water, and a probe hole opens a path out.

The dogs came from the New South Wales Police Force canine unit. Two were English springer spaniels, aged three and seven and a half, and one was a four-year-old Labrador retriever.

The youngest had about a year of experience and the oldest about six.

None had worked a buried body before. Each dog was released off leash about 500 feet (150 meters) from the grave, from a different direction each visit, and alerted by lying down or barking.

The handlers didn’t know where the grave was on the first visit, but the head trainer did, and watched from a distance to rule on each alert.

The electronic nose, called NOS.E, carries five gas sensors tuned to the chemical families that buried bodies release, such as alcohols and compounds containing nitrogen or sulfur.

Sources indicate that before each dog ran, a researcher walked it over the grave with its intake about 6 inches (15 centimeters) above the ground. An empty control grave 16 feet (5 meters) away was sampled the same way.

After probing, every dog tested alerted over the donor’s upper torso, where the device registered its strongest readings.

Over the whole trial, the sensors for nitrogen and sulfur compounds and for alcohols responded most.

Industry observers note that the two younger dogs each gave a false alert during searches before probing. The oldest dog never gave a false alert.

Once the grave was probed, no dog missed it and none alerted in the wrong place.

Air samples sent to a lab confirmed the same chemical families were present on every search day. They surged after heavy rain and a warm spell around days 126 and 147.

With so few alerts to compare, the statistics could not confirm a link between sensor strength and correct alerts, though correct alerts tended to come with higher readings.

Brown said the device could give trainers another way to check whether a dog’s alert coincides with a chemical signal consistent with decomposition.

“For younger dogs in particular, the technology could help trainers determine whether a dog is genuinely responding to decomposition odor or being influenced by another cue,” she remarked.

According to recent reports, the device is not meant to replace the dogs. A dog covers ground promptly and smells things no sensor array can, while the device uses sensors that respond to broad groups of chemicals.

On the last day the probe punctured the remains, and every sensor fired at once on gases a normal search would never release.

One donor, buried at one depth in one season, is the whole dataset.

The dogs may have learned where the grave was over six visits, even though they started from different spots each time.

And the device has not been tested against other soils, deeper burials, or mixed smells, so it is not ready for a real search.

Whether a dog alerts to a single compound, a mix, or a concentration is still the open question.

Recent findings suggest that ueland’s team prepares a larger study with several donors and more dogs over repeated visits. The hard part, she said, will be keeping the dogs and handlers from learning the sites.

Until that study runs, the pairing has been tried on one grave, and there the sensors and the dogs agreed.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

#157367. Tech Report: An armored amphibian hunted like a shark 237 million years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1132 w)

Tech Report: An armored amphibian hunted like a shark 237 million years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two fossils from southern China reveal an armored amphibian that lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago.
  • No living amphibian is known to spend its entire life in the open ocean.
  • Yet in the Late Triassic, a flat, armored amphibian about 2½ feet (75 centimeters) long lived on the sea floor at least 19 miles (30 kilometers) from the nearest land.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two fossils from southern China reveal an armored amphibian that lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago.

No living amphibian is known to spend its entire life in the open ocean. For most, seawater draws moisture out through their permeable skin.

Yet in the Late Triassic, a flat, armored amphibian about 2½ feet (75 centimeters) long lived on the sea floor at least 19 miles (30 kilometers) from the nearest land.

Two nearly complete skeletons from southern China provide the first evidence of an amphibian that lived entirely at sea.

Industry observers note that the researchers named the species Gerrothorax maritimus. The name maritimus means “of the sea.”.

Their case rests on where the bones lay and what they are made of, plus a suit of armor the animal’s freshwater ancestors already wore.

The fossils were studied by Lipin Diao of the Geological Museum of Guizhou, Ryosuke Motani of the University of California, Davis, and Da-yong Jiang of Peking University, with two colleagues.

“If you think about today’s amphibians, this animal is unusual because it’s massive,” Motani noted.

“It’s probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what’s different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky.”.

Local fossil collectors dug the skeletons out of a quarry in Guanling County, Guizhou Province, in 2004.

It has been revealed that the bones went to the Geological Museum of Guizhou in 2022, when it opened as the province’s official fossil repository. The rock around them is about 237 million years old.

The same bed has produced large ocean-going ichthyosaurs, animals of the open sea. In the Late Triassic, this rock was the floor of a gulf about 125 miles (200 kilometers) from any large landmass.

The bones argue against a carcass that drifted out from a river. The larger skeleton still has its fingers in place, and fingers are among the first parts a dead four-legged animal loses at sea.

“Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom,” remarked Motani, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences.

“But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived.”.

Strontium is a metal that animals take in with their water and build into bone. The mix of its forms differs between the open ocean and water that drains off land.

The team measured that mix in dense bone from both skeletons and in the rock around them.

Sources indicate that the bone values were close to the global seawater value of the time. The surrounding rock read higher, closer to the older rocks of the nearby land.

The two skeletons also agreed with each other far more closely than the rock samples did, which the authors read as a living body controlling its own chemistry.

In an interview with Earth.com, Motani remarked the strontium result needed little interpretation.

“I was surprised to see a clean result, which did not require a lot of interpretations to say A or B,” he said.

Amphibians breathe and drink through their skin, and that’s what fails them in the ocean, Motani remarked.

A few living species can tolerate brackish water, and some can even withstand brief exposure to seawater.

“This wonderful device, however, does not do its job in sea water and instead works against the animal,” Motani told Earth.com.

According to recent reports, gerrothorax had a way around that long before it reached the sea. Its back was covered in a pavement of bony plates about an inch across and less than a fifth of an inch thick.

In a recent development, A second layer of bony rods and small plates protected the belly. The lineage also kept internal gills into adulthood, which most living amphibians lose.

It has been revealed that the researchers propose that the armor limited water exchange through the skin. If so, the animal may have taken in water by drinking seawater and shed excess salt through its gills, much as marine fish do.

The armor evolved in fresh water as protection from predators, Motani mentioned, and happened to be the right equipment for a later move into the sea.

“There was a freshwater amphibian that happened to have the equipment needed to colonize the sea – the body armor,” he mentioned.

The larger skeleton is 29 inches (74 centimeters) long as preserved. The skull is only about 5 inches (13 centimeters) long but close to 10 inches (25 centimeters) wide. The armored back reaches about 11 inches (29 centimeters) across.

Sources indicate that the animal’s hind legs are longer than its front legs. The authors read that as a sign it breathed with gills rather than lungs, since lung-breathing sea animals usually need longer front legs to stay balanced in the water.

The throat bones are heavily built, as strong as those of sharks that feed by suction. So the team pictures a flat animal resting on the bottom, like a wobbegong carpet shark, and swallowing whatever swam too close.

“They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in,” Motani stated.

The salt-handling system and the feeding style are inferences from bone, since no soft tissue survived.

According to recent reports, nobody knows whether these ancient amphibians had permeable skin like a frog’s. Nor do the fossils say whether Gerrothorax maritimus laid eggs or gave birth to live young, and amphibian eggs do poorly in salt water.

The species also lived in a greenhouse world, much warmer than today’s.

Even a return to those temperatures would probably not open the sea to modern amphibians, the authors wrote, because most of them lose their gills as adults.

Land vertebrates have colonized the ocean roughly 70 times, and this is the only amphibian lineage known to have gone all the way.

Asked by Earth.com where more marine amphibians might turn up, Motani pointed to Triassic marine shales laid down in the tropics of the time.

Sources indicate that the best bet, he said, is near where the ancient Panthalassa and Tethys oceans met. Those rocks are where this one came from, and where China’s Triassic marine reptiles keep appearing.

Whether Gerrothorax maritimus was alone in the sea, or the first of several armored relatives to make the crossing, is the question those shales will have to answer.

Until a second one turns up, the whole case for a marine amphibian rests on two skeletons from one quarry.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.

Sources indicate that the unit heats and cools with 24,000 BTUs of power, which is more than enough, but considering the model's premium price, it's a little on the low side. Its SEER rating is 20.5, and operation is relatively quiet.

Overall, it’s a great package, albeit a pricey one.

In a recent development, compared to window or portable air conditioners, ductless systems are more permanent, more powerful, and typically quieter. They also give you more control over specific rooms, so you can cool the spaces you actually use instead of the whole house at once. There are some drawbacks, though.

Ductless ACs run pricey (even setting aside the cost of installation). They’re also more visible than central air vents, and you need to size and place them carefully to cool a room evenly. DIY installs or wrong-sized units can cause complications in the long run.

Maintenance can also be difficult, as not all HVAC professionals are familiar with these products. However, for an older home with radiator heat (like mine is), it’s the best way to add efficient air conditioning without blocking most of our windows.

It has been revealed that first, decide how many indoor units you need and where you’ll place them. Unlike window units, mini-split systems are permanent fixtures, so carefully consider where they’ll be most efficient within your home.

Sources indicate that generally, a single ductless air conditioner can handle cooling a targeted area or a single room. If you’re cooling down multiple rooms, consider a multi-zone system so that you get even temperatures throughout your home.

Industry observers note that it’s also essential to select a unit that’s powerful enough for the room it’s in—too small and it may not cool your space. The cooling capacity of air conditioners is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTUs, per hour.

In a recent development, as a general rule of thumb, choose a unit that delivers 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. So, a 200-square-foot room needs at least a 4,000-BTU air conditioner. Those sensitive to noise should consider units with a quiet mode feature.

According to recent reports, it’s also key to consider the electrical system in the area you initiative to install the mini-split. Many larger mini-splits require 208- to 230-volt power, which works with both commercial 208V electrical service and the 240V circuits typically used for major appliances in homes, while smaller systems may run on standard 120V outlets without any needed upgrades.

In a recent development, quieter units are more desirable for bedrooms, living rooms, and nurseries, where a peaceful environment is essential. Look for ductless air conditioners with noise levels between 19 and 30 decibels, since this range can be compared to the sound of leaves rustling or a soft whisper.

Units with levels between 30 to 40 decibels are still suitable for other areas of the home, since this range is comparable to background noise or casual conversation.

While shopping for your ductless air conditioner, you may see “SEER” with a number next to it. SEER stands for Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, which measures how much energy your air conditioner uses during the annual cooling season. The higher the SEER rating, the less energy your unit uses to cool your home.

You may also see “SEER2,” a newer efficiency standard introduced in 2023 that uses updated testing conditions meant to better reflect real-world performance. SEER2 numbers are typically slightly lower than SEER ratings for the same unit, but they represent the same idea: higher numbers mean more efficient energy usage.

A product with an Energy Star certification has been rigorously tested by the United States Environmental Protection Agency for its energy efficiency. EPA-recognized laboratories test products to Energy Star specifications to ensure manufacturers produce energy-saving products.

Although testing guidelines change per product category, all items must prove they consume less energy than standard models without compromising performance.

Recent findings suggest that mini-splits are more permanent and expensive than window or portable air conditioners, so they make the most sense when you plan to cool the same space for several seasons. Most systems also require professional installation, and larger units may need electrical upgrades before you can install them.

They’re also not invisible. The indoor air handler usually stays mounted high on the wall year-round, which may bother homeowners who prefer the low-profile look of central air vents. Proper sizing and placement matter, too, since an oversized, undersized, or poorly positioned unit can lead to uneven cooling, wasted energy, or poor humidity control.

Ductless air conditioners cool your home without using the network of ducts that central HVAC systems rely on, claims Lincoln. “The way I explain ductless cooling to homeowners is simple: the system conditions the room directly instead of trying to send cooled air through ductwork first,” she explains.

Sources indicate that instead, ductless air conditioners connect a small outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers using refrigerant lines. Because there’s no ductwork involved, these types of units are often more efficient and easier to install in older homes, additions, or finished spaces where running ducts would be difficult. They also allow for “zoned” cooling, meaning you can control the temperature in individual rooms instead of conditioning the entire house at once.

According to recent reports, these systems are also more customizable than a whole-house system. “Where mini-splits really shine is zoning,” explains Lincoln. “One outdoor unit can support multiple indoor heads, so different parts of the house can be conditioned based on how those spaces are actually used.”.

Yes. “A mini-split is just a ductless system made up of an outdoor condenser and one or more indoor air handlers,” indicates Lincoln. The terms ductless air conditioner and mini-split are generally used interchangeably, as we have in this guide.

Both describe systems that pair an outdoor condenser with one or more indoor air handlers connected by refrigerant lines instead of ductwork. The “split” part refers to the system being divided between indoor and outdoor components.

According to recent reports, some mini-splits provide cooling only, but many modern models are actually heat pumps, meaning they can both cool and heat your home using the same system. Adding air conditioning to an older home that previously utilized radiator or baseboard heat can be tricky—squeezing ductwork into closets and unused corners feels a bit like remodelling Jenga. These units solve that matter without much fuss.

Usually, yes. In most cases, it makes sense to hire a professional. Installing a mini-split usually involves mounting indoor and outdoor units, running refrigerant lines, and making electrical connections, which is why many manufacturers recommend professional installation.

In a recent development, “Installation is where good equipment gets made—or wasted,” advises Lincoln. “Mini-splits look deceptively simple once they’re on the wall, but installation is not casual work. Line sets, electrical, drainage, vacuuming the system down properly before startup…those are the steps that determine whether the unit runs the way it was engineered to run.”.

It has been revealed that some systems are more DIY-friendly, but even those can be complicated if you’re not comfortable working with electrical systems or HVAC equipment. Professional installation also helps ensure the system runs efficiently and may be required to maintain the manufacturer’s warranty. If you are a very seasoned DIY pro who’s handy with a YouTube tutorial, you might be okay. Otherwise, we recommend budgeting for an installer.

Companies size mini-splits systems based on BTUs, which measure how much heating or cooling power the unit can deliver.

“When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close. For a mini-split, a proper load calculation is the better answer.” This is another reason it’s great to work with an expert installer before ordering—they can guide your purchasing based on your needs.

Lincoln explains that it’s not a straightforward calculation, in most cases. “Room size is only the starting point. Sun exposure, ceiling height, insulation, window size, window direction, occupancy, and heat from electronics or appliances all change the cooling load,” she adds.

Smaller systems around 9,000 BTU often work for bedrooms or small offices, while 12,000–18,000-BTU systems handle larger living areas. As a rough rule, most homeowners look at units sized for the square footage of the space they want to heat or cool, but must consider all of these other factors, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

Sources indicate that the animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, indicates Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

Recent findings suggest that the answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin claims. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she notes. But that’s not what the team discovered.

Recent findings suggest that in separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.).

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin claims. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she indicates, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, coastal mangrove forests are critical for protecting shorelines from severe storms and trapping CO2. Unfortunately, they are losing the race against rising sea levels.

Mangrove forests grow right at the edge of the sea, so rising water can drown them. To survive, the ground under the trees has to build up as fast as the ocean rises. A latest study finds that dead seagrass helps that happen.

Before sunrise on his monthly survey days, from May 2022 to May 2024, Florida International University (FIU) doctoral student Kevin Montenegro loaded a 16-foot (4.9-meter) canoe onto a truck and set off to paddle for an hour to the Biscayne Bay mangroves.

He then waded in to see what the tide had left. Much of it was dead seagrass and macroalgae, the debris that scientists call “marine wrack.”.

When seagrass washes into a mangrove forest, it adds material to the forest floor and traps carbon that would otherwise warm the climate.

An isotope model estimated that seagrass supplied between 36 and 53 percent of the soil carbon near the surface at his two sites, according to FIU. It has not closed the gap, because the sea there is rising at least twice as fast as the ground.

It has been revealed that montenegro and a field partner worked at two sites in Biscayne National Park, on the Atlantic coast of Florida. The paper calls them BISC-1 and BISC-2. They lie about 5 miles (8 kilometers) apart, in a narrow band of forest along the shore.

BISC-1, the southern site, sits just south of the mouth of the Homestead Military Canal and east of the L-31E levee, built in 1966.

BISC-2 sits near the mouth of the Black Creek Canal, in the Cutler Wetlands, where roads and urban development run beside the shore.

Levees and roads stop these mangroves from moving inland, and little river sediment reaches them.

The National Park Service set up both monitoring stations with a surface elevation table, an instrument that records small changes in ground height from a fixed benchmark.

The readings run from February 2011 at BISC-1 and January 2012 at BISC-2 through September 2024. BISC-1 has 25 rounds of measurements and BISC-2 has 23.

Sea level in the bay is rising about 8.5 millimeters (0.33 inch) a year, based on data from the NOAA tide gauge at Virginia Key.

The ground at BISC-1 rose about 2.1 millimeters (0.08 inch) a year, and the ground at BISC-2 rose about 3.9 millimeters (0.15 inch).

Industry observers note that that left BISC-1 about 6.4 millimeters (0.25 inch) short each year. Below the surface, the land at BISC-1 sank 0.7 millimeters a year and the land at BISC-2 sank 0.4.

Hurricane Irma hit the area in 2017. Elevation at both sites had climbed sharply until 2014, declined from 2014 to 2019, and has risen steadily since 2018, possibly from new plant growth and sediment moved by the storm, the authors wrote.

Sources indicate that yearly gains are 1.1 millimeters higher at BISC-1 and 2.2 higher at BISC-2 than in the last regional synthesis. Other research has warned that Florida’s mangroves may end up underwater as seas climb.

It has been revealed that montenegro made 23 monthly wrack surveys between May 2022 and May 2024. He and his partner marked three lines at each site, each one 66 feet (20 meters) long, and stopped at the shoreline, at 33 feet and at 66 feet.

At every stop they laid down a frame of about 11 square feet (1 square meter), wrote down how much seagrass, macroalgae, plastic, wood and mangrove litter lay inside it, and measured the pile with a meter stick. Then they photographed it.

According to recent reports, researchers usually study wrack on beaches, FIU stated, since they can walk up to it or see it from satellites. Neither works well under a mangrove canopy.

For the decomposition test, the team filled nylon bags with about 5 grams of red mangrove leaves or the seagrass Thalassia testudinum.

They left the bags on the soil and collected them after six and 12 months, then repeated the experiment for a second year.

The surveys also caught a regional event. Sargassum, a brown macroalga, reached its highest level on the plots in March 2023, the same month the University of South Florida‘s satellite system reported a peak across the region.

It has been revealed that south Florida’s mangroves are generally thought to build soil from their own leaves, wood and roots, according to FIU. The team pulled soil cores 4 inches (10 centimeters) deep during four sampling rounds and removed the roots where possible.

They then measured stable isotopes, forms of carbon and nitrogen that differ between plant sources, and ran a statistical model that compared the soil with red mangrove and seagrass tissue.

In the top 0.8 inch (2 centimeters), the seagrass share ranged from 36.1 percent at the innermost point of BISC-1 to 53 percent at the same point of BISC-2.

BISC-2, in the Cutler Wetlands, received more than 3.4 times as much wrack as BISC-1 at 66 feet inland, and its ground rose fastest. The seagrass share fell lower down the cores, likely because roots add more material at depth.

Where more wrack piled up, seagrass in the bags broke down more slowly at both sites, and mangrove leaves did the same at BISC-2.

Past measurements at the stations recorded single wrack deposits adding between 0.07 and 1.8 inches (1.78 and 46.38 millimeters) to the surface.

Montenegro knew both habitats before the project began. As an FIU undergraduate he worked in a seagrass lab that studied water quality damage, and he later measured mangrove elevation with the National Park Service.

Sources indicate that “We know seagrass ecosystems are very sensitive to water quality,” he said in the FIU release. Losing those meadows, he added, would mean “losing a huge contributor to mangrove resilience.”.

It has been revealed that the bay is one where climate stress has already changed the water. Mangroves worldwide also face a triple threat to their survival, and rising seas may push some forests to release stored carbon.

Sources indicate that the authors wrote that management and restoration efforts should consider strategies that protect the route that carries wrack from seagrass beds into the forests. Montenegro called mangroves and seagrass “puzzle pieces that make our community whole.”.

The study covers two sites in one national park, and the elevation rates carry wide error margins, plus or minus 2.6 millimeters a year at BISC-1 and 3.2 at BISC-2.

Seasonal wrack volume tracked surface elevation change at both sites, but it showed no clear relationship with the soil accumulation measured above marker layers.

The authors wrote that wrack volume alone was not driving those patterns, and proposed slower decay and added peat as the route.

Their model also used only two sources, red mangrove and Thalassia testudinum, so it did not separate the macroalgae found on the plots.

Water depth has climbed sharply at both sites since 2019, and the authors warned that longer flooding could eventually starve roots of oxygen.

The National Park Service funded the work under agreement P21AC11346-00, and two of the four authors, Kevin Whelan and Michelle Prats, work for its South Florida and Caribbean monitoring network.

Montenegro finished his Ph.D. earlier this year and now works in the Department of Environmental Resources Management for Miami-Dade County, on the same coast where he once loaded a canoe before sunrise.

The full study was published in the journal Estuaries and Coasts.

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s newly introduced voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”.

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

Sources indicate that in her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

In a recent development, the race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Recent findings suggest that calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

Industry observers note that one incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Industry observers note that two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.
