According to recent reports, whether you want small or large ice cubes for your favorite beverages, the Kenmore Top Load Ice Maker delivers both, making it a strong first foray into ice makers if you’re still on the fence. This machine makes nine bullet-shaped cubes in about seven minutes, and there are two different sizes to choose from. The top-load design and included scoop make grabbing ice a breeze.

This model comes with a carrying handle, making it a more portable option than other countertop ice makers we’ve tried. The self-cleaning mode and bottom drain allow for more simplified maintenance. You need to let it sit upright for 24 hours before your first use, so make sure you account for that before you need your ice.

Consider your ice cube style preference when deciding on a countertop ice maker. Most machines do not pop out the crystal-clear ice you’d find at a top-tier restaurant or bar. Instead, some of the most popular shapes are nugget ice cubes, also known as pellets or Sonic. Soft and chewable, this style is the cube of choice at restaurants like Sonic and Chick-fil-A, but the cubes melt swiftly, and the machines that make them tend to be more expensive due to their popularity. Also, consider if you’ll want different ice sizes for different drinks. Many machines offer two cube sizes—a smaller one good for sodas and iced coffees and a larger option more suited for cocktails. If you blueprint to make both, look for one of these.

It has been revealed that there isn’t much of a difference in size among the best countertop ice makers. Some space-savers are tall and narrow, while others are lower and deep, ideal to fit beneath a kitchen cabinet. At most, countertop ice makers range from roughly 10 to 15 inches deep and 12 to 17 inches high.

Sources indicate that most countertop ice makers designed for kitchens produce 26 pounds of ice in 24 hours. This is more than enough for households with four to six people, assuming there are no major ice demands (like a party). Larger households or offices may appreciate a more productive machine that churns out 30 or more pounds of ice per day.

Countertop ice makers either use water from a built-in reservoir or a connected water line, but the former is most common. You’ll need to refill a reservoir ice maker with water when it runs out. The major benefit is it doesn’t require any plumbing connections—you just fill the tank and it’s ready to use. Just keep in mind that most machines recommend using filtered water to prevent mineral deposits from building up.

In a recent development, if your ice maker will be running all the time and you don’t want to hear constant humming and clinking, look for a model that produces 40 decibels of sound or less. Some ice makers automatically run when they sense the basket is running low on ice—keep this in mind if you prefer a quieter machine.

Self-cleaning is an key feature to consider and look for, as cleaning a countertop ice maker requires dumping ice and removing and replacing several components. With a simple click of a button, you know your machine is clean and the ice tastes fresh. After all, using the best quality ice amplifies the taste of your beverages, too.

Industry observers note that yes, whether you hook your ice maker up to a water line or use a refillable tank, you can keep it supplied with tap water. However, if you find that your tap water has an unpleasant flavor, you may prefer to use filtered water.

Yes, it’s perfectly safe to leave most ice makers on during the day and night. Of course, if you’re not using the ice, you will be using electricity to keep it running.

Recent findings suggest that some countertop ice makers require a water hookup. This means you’ll need to place the machine near some plumbing in your kitchen. If this isn’t an option for your home, however, many of the machines we love use a refillable water reservoir instead of, or in addition to, a water line.

High school and college teams can win up to $20,000 each by designing technology for NASA’s Moon Base, and sign-ups close January 25

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that NASA's Moon Base Challenge invites U.S.
  • The Moon Base Challenge was declared on November 8 at a MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida.
  • It has been revealed that teams do not need prior specialized engineering or technical experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that NASA's Moon Base Challenge invites U.S. high school and college teams to design technology for a lunar base.

The Moon Base Challenge was declared on November 8 at a MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. It is open to student teams at U.S. high schools and post-secondary schools.

It has been revealed that teams do not need prior specialized engineering or technical experience. In the final round, they can explain an idea with a mock-up made of cardboard. Students have helped with real research before, as when students helped astronomers track a rare alien comet.

NASA is building a Moon Base where astronauts will live, work and explore in the lunar South Pole region. The agency says a permanent human presence on the Moon paves the way for future crewed missions to Mars.

In a recent development, the region may contain resources that could one day help support explorers. NASA aims to send a nuclear-powered rover called PROMISE to search for evidence of water ice and other resources there.

“We’re looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA’s future on the Moon,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute.”.

“Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we’re looking for,” mentioned Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program.

Each team picks one of six categories: power generation and storage, habitat construction using lunar materials, life-support systems, surface mobility, communication networks, or astronaut safety.

Habitat ideas can go beyond engineering, since researchers have argued that Moon bases could be designed to ease anxiety and homesickness.

The designs have to work in a harsh place. According to the official rules, they must handle vacuum, radiation, micrometeorites, abrasive dust and temperature swings from 248 degrees Fahrenheit (120 degrees Celsius) to minus 274 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 170 degrees Celsius).

They also have to cope with day and night cycles that last two weeks each, and rely as little as possible on supplies from Earth.

Water is one of the hard parts: one analysis found that the Moon can generate enough power for a permanent city, but not enough water.

A team has two to five students and an adult coach, at least 18, who holds a formal role at the team’s school or organization, such as a teacher, faculty member or club advisor.

There are three divisions, judged separately. High school teams are for students in grades 9 to 12 who were between 13 and 18 years old when registration opened, including home-schooled students.

The other two divisions are for undergraduates at two-year schools, such as community and technical colleges, and at four-year colleges and universities.

Those students must be at least 16. A mixed team competes in the division of its most advanced or oldest member. Middle school and graduate students cannot take part.

Recent findings suggest that students must be U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents or foreign nationals who are full-time students at an eligible U.S. school and physically live in the United States for the whole challenge.

Every student has to create an account on NASA’s STEM Gateway, and only the student team lead submits the application. Coaches should not register there; they are linked to the team later on the organizer’s platform.

In a recent development, in the first phase, teams write a Concept Overview Paper of 5 to 7 pages. It must explain how the idea works and how it survives lunar conditions, and include at least one page of diagrams or other visuals. Papers are due February 22, 2027.

Up to 100 teams will be named finalists on March 11. They will then record a pitch video of up to 10 minutes, with a deck of up to 15 slides, due April 19.

Finalists can explain their design with hand-drawn diagrams, posterboard schematics or low-cost mock-ups made of cardboard, foam or household materials. CAD software and physical prototypes are allowed but optional. Winners will be unveiled on May 6, 2027.

NASA’s announcement calls it a $1 million challenge, and the challenge website claims up to $1 million in monetary awards are available.

The official rules for the 2026-27 challenge, however, list a total maximum prize payout of $500,000, and neither source explains the difference.

Recent findings suggest that each of up to 100 finalist teams gets $1,400. In the final phase, up to 12 grand prize winners get $20,000 each, and up to 12 runners-up get $10,000 each.

The rules also say payments depend on federal funding and NASA’s final approval, and NASA does not have to award the full amount if too few entries meet its quality bar.

Sources indicate that the money goes to a U.S. bank account designated by the team’s coach, who decides how it is shared. Teams keep the rights to what they invent, although NASA may negotiate a license to use it.

In a recent development, A virtual opening symposium introducing the categories is set for December 3. Registered teams can also join live question-and-answer webinars on January 14 and February 11, 2027. The organizers say all dates may change.

Sources indicate that the challenge is run for NASA by the Institute of Competition Sciences. Full rules and registration steps are on the official challenge website.

The information was obtained from NASA’s announcement, its Moon Base page and the official rules.

  • Significant thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Anna Mattson and Science News Staff.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor.

Significant thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” says senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a latest appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”.

Recent findings suggest that staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with latest parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús indicates. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”.

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Manufacturer | $29.99.

Adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham notes.

Saul Justin NewmanThe MIT Press | $29.95.

Senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen indicates. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”.

Susana CarmonaThe MIT Press | $27.95.

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, new mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she says. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Aaron MahnkeRunning Press | $30.00.

Those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century Fresh England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

For the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”.

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00.

Recent findings suggest that conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover indicates. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole new light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”.

It has been revealed that riley BlackSt. Martin’s Press | $29.00.

Tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” says Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”.

Joshua D. MezrichThe MIT Press | $29.95.

And for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”.

#157348. Breaking: Traces of insecticide in cord blood raise newly introduced questions about childhood development

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1214 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Traces of insecticide in cord blood raise newly introduced questions about childhood development

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Japanese study linked insecticide exposure before a child's birth to lower scores on certain thinking tests at age nine.
  • Two compounds linked to widely used insecticides turned up in umbilical cord blood in a Japanese study.
  • At age 9, children with higher levels of one compound at birth scored lower on a test of processing speed, while those with higher levels of the other scored lower on a test of visual reasoning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Japanese study linked insecticide exposure before a child's birth to lower scores on certain thinking tests at age nine.

Two compounds linked to widely used insecticides turned up in umbilical cord blood in a Japanese study.

At age 9, children with higher levels of one compound at birth scored lower on a test of processing speed, while those with higher levels of the other scored lower on a test of visual reasoning.

Earlier tests, given between 10 and 32 months, yielded no clear links after researchers accounted for the number of comparisons they made.

It has been revealed that the researchers wrote that any association may hinge on the age of the child and the skill examined. Just 200 children took part. Proof that the insecticides caused the weaker scores cannot be drawn from this work.

Abir Nagata and Kenji Tsuchiya, a professor, headed the investigation. Both are based at the Research Center for Child Mental Development at Hamamatsu University School of Medicine.

They are also affiliated with a graduate school run jointly by The University of Osaka and four other Japanese universities.

The growth of a child’s brain and abilities is referred to by scientists as neurodevelopment. Children in earlier work on these insecticides were seldom followed beyond early childhood.

“Previous studies have largely focused on neurodevelopmental outcomes at a single time point,” Nagata said.

Industry observers note that nicotine served as the chemical model for neonicotinoids. Their target is a receptor on nerve cells that normally binds one of the body’s chemical messengers.

Insects carry these receptors and so do humans. Within a fetus, the authors wrote, the receptors assist nerve cells in maturing and connecting.

Harm to bees is what the insecticides are chiefly known for. Over a quarter of global insecticide sales are now attributed to them.

Food and drinking water have both been found to contain residues. Nationwide monitoring in Japan has picked up neonicotinoids in tap water throughout the year.

It has been revealed that animal experiments have been cited as grounds for concern. Altered brain structure followed exposure during brain development in those experiments. Impaired movement, learning and attention were documented as well.

Links with early development have been reported in several studies of children. Agreement between those studies has been poor, however.

Industry observers note that all of the children are enrolled in the Hamamatsu Birth Cohort, an ongoing project on child development. The project recruited 1,258 babies. Their births took place in Hamamatsu, Japan, between December 2007 and March 2012.

Urine from pregnant women was the usual source of insecticide measurements in earlier research. What actually reached the baby in the womb is not shown directly by urine. Umbilical cord blood drawn at birth offers a direct measure.

Limited resources meant that cord blood from only 200 randomly selected children could be analyzed. Serum, the liquid fraction of blood, was screened by a laboratory for insecticides and their breakdown products.

Industry observers note that of the ten compounds measured, just two turned up often. Dinotefuran was detected in 104 of the 200 samples, or 52%.

A breakdown product of acetamiprid, a second insecticide, was the other. Its detection rate was 62.5%, or 125 samples.

Recent findings suggest that the team split the children into low, middle and high groups for each of the two chemicals. Detection was seldom possible in the low group, which was used as the comparison.

Quantities were minute. A typical reading in the high dinotefuran group was 0.07 billionths of a gram per milliliter of serum.

It has been revealed that the researchers scheduled five rounds of testing between 10 and 32 months of age. Depending on the visit, 185 to 195 children had enough data to be included in the analysis.

Sources indicate that toddlers with higher levels scored below the low group in a handful of comparisons. Large body movements at 10 and 14 months were weaker in the middle dinotefuran group.

In a recent development, the reverse was seen once. Hand and finger skills at 18 months were stronger in the middle group for the acetamiprid breakdown product.

The team ran 50 comparisons per chemical over the toddler period. Some results will appear meaningful purely by chance when that many comparisons are run.

Statistical significance was lost for every toddler result after the researchers corrected for this. Across ages and skills, no consistent pattern emerged.

It has been revealed that A standard four-part intelligence test was completed by 178 of the 200 children at age 9. Differences on two of the four parts survived the same correction.

Sources indicate that processing speed was lower among children in the middle dinotefuran group. The measure captures how fast a child gets through simple tasks.

The shortfall against the low group came to roughly 7 points. An average score on this test is 100.

Perceptual reasoning was weaker in the high group for the acetamiprid breakdown product. Visual puzzles and pattern spotting are what this part of the test relies on. The gap on this part was almost as wide.

Overall IQ scores were lower in those same two groups as well.

It has been revealed that rising insecticide levels did not bring a steady decline in scores. Processing speed was also lower in the high dinotefuran group. That difference was smaller, though, and chance could account for it.

Recent findings suggest that tsuchiya said the contrast with the toddler findings may reflect links specific to certain skills and ages. On that reading, no single lasting pattern runs through childhood.

According to recent reports, the children were only observed as they grew up, and nothing about their exposure was controlled. A link can therefore be identified by the study, whereas a cause cannot be proven.

A single blood sample taken at delivery supplied each child’s insecticide level. The timing of exposure during pregnancy cannot be learned from one sample. Neither can the degree to which exposure varied.

Adjustments were made for each child’s sex and age, premature birth and the education of both parents.

Diet went unmeasured, as did lead, other heavy metals and the parents’ own thinking skills. Part of the gap in scores might be explained by such factors.

According to recent reports, dinotefuran levels at birth were also higher in children who took the age 9 test than in the rest. The results could be skewed by that difference.

Too few samples contained the eight other compounds for them to be analyzed, alone or combined.

Only 178 children contributed to the age 9 results. The authors wrote that estimates from a sample of this size are imprecise. Weaker links may also have gone undetected.

Whether other groups of children show the same links is the next question. Why the links would surface at age 9 and not sooner also remains unexplained.

The authors called for larger studies. Exposure would need to be measured several times during pregnancy in such studies. Testing of the children would continue through middle childhood.

For now, a single group of children in one Japanese city is the source of the evidence.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association indicates it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart challenges, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

According to recent reports, they also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

As a top name in yard tools, we are interested to see what Toro’s take on simple snow removal is.

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

Ego has several models of electric now shovels. This one has adjustable fins to let you guide the direction of the snow you remove.

It has been revealed that we leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

According to recent reports, with a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it rolls out snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

According to recent reports, you may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

In a recent development, just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

Industry observers note that for reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was rapidly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

According to recent reports, we must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Sources indicate that overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

Sources indicate that the lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

Sources indicate that with its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

Sources indicate that the two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That noted, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

In a recent development, electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you initiative to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

According to recent reports, electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Industry observers note that electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

In a recent development, similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side.

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It has been revealed that it’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

In a recent development, soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

According to recent reports, house Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

According to recent reports, soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

Sources indicate that “Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida revealed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto mentioned in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”.

Recent findings suggest that while Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

#157345. Glaciers lose ice faster where they meet lakes, but there’s more to the story

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1457 w)

Glaciers lose ice faster where they meet lakes, but there’s more to the story

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Glaciers that end in lakes lost ice about 65% faster than those that end on land, but climate and terrain explained more of the variation than lakes did.
  • Meltwater is often collected in the hollow that a retreating glacier leaves behind.
  • It has been revealed that once such a lake has formed, the neighboring ice can be lost more quickly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Glaciers that end in lakes lost ice about 65% faster than those that end on land, but climate and terrain explained more of the variation than lakes did.

Meltwater is often collected in the hollow that a retreating glacier leaves behind.

It has been revealed that once such a lake has formed, the neighboring ice can be lost more quickly. The lake melts the glacier front below the waterline, and pieces break off more easily.

The size of that effect has now been estimated across the world’s glaciers by an international team. Between 2000 and 2020, glaciers ending in lakes were found to lose ice about 65% faster than those on land.

Industry observers note that in the researchers’ model, lake characteristics accounted for about 11% of the differences in ice loss the model could explain. Climate and glacier terrain accounted for most of the rest.

Recent findings suggest that the work was led by Shaochun Zhao and Guoqing Zhang. Both are at the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Their 15 co-authors work in China, Europe, and the United States. One of them is Tobias Bolch of the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology.

The team worked from satellite images and a statistical model. No instruments were placed at the ice.

In a recent development, glacial lakes were mapped everywhere outside Antarctica using images from the Landsat satellites. The images were taken around 2000 and again around 2020.

Sources indicate that software trained to recognize lakes drew the first outlines. Those outlines were then checked and corrected by eye.

A lake had to cover about two-thirds of an acre (0.0027 square kilometers) to count.

Glacial lakes of every kind increased 9% in number, to 160,332. Lakes touching a glacier increased 35%, a gain of 3,567 lakes.

Three-quarters of the water added to glacial lakes went into lakes touching ice.

According to recent reports, the team estimated that lakes in direct contact with glaciers held about 16 cubic miles (66 cubic kilometers) more water by 2020. Volume was worked out from surface area with the help of depth surveys of 299 lakes.

Industry observers note that bolch’s university put that volume in city terms. Poured over Vienna in an even layer, the water would stand about 525 feet (160 meters) deep.

Worldwide growth of glacial lakes since 1990 had already been documented in the same journal by a 2020 survey.

In that survey, however, lakes were not sorted according to whether they touch ice. That detail was required for the present study.

Industry observers note that expansion of ice-touching lakes by more than 39 square miles (100 square kilometers) was recorded in only two regions. These were Alaska and the southern Andes. Fifteen of the 20 lakes with the largest growth are located in these two regions.

According to recent reports, the largest single gain, roughly 20 square miles (53 square kilometers), was measured at a lake in Alaska. Within the southern Andes, growth was concentrated around the two Patagonian ice fields.

Most of the growth came from a small number of large lakes. Although 2,946 lakes expanded in total, 810 of them grew by more than 25 acres (0.1 square kilometers).

Those 810 lakes accounted for 92% of the total area gain.

A further 4,538 ice-touching lakes were formed between 2000 and 2020.

It has been revealed that contact with the ice was not maintained everywhere. During the same period, 1,645 lakes became detached from their glaciers. In New Zealand, eight lakes were detached while only three new ones were formed.

Industry observers note that to compare glaciers, the team relied on the Randolph Glacier Inventory, a global catalog of glacier outlines. It was combined with an existing record of glacier ice loss.

Of roughly 214,000 glaciers, 7,121 terminate in a lake and 1,512 in the sea, while the remainder end on land.

Recent findings suggest that ice loss is expressed by glaciologists as a depth of water. This is the depth the lost ice would produce if spread across the whole glacier.

By that measure, lake-ending glaciers lost about 26 inches (0.66 meters) a year.

For land-ending glaciers the figure was about 16 inches (0.40 meters), and for sea-ending glaciers about 14 inches (0.36 meters).

Bolch was part of a team that found a similar gap among Himalayan glaciers in 2019.

It has been revealed that the fastest ice loss was not seen at these glaciers everywhere. In Iceland, Svalbard, the Russian Arctic, and northern Arctic Canada, they lost less ice than land-ending ones.

Industry observers note that A possible reason was suggested by the authors. Lake-ending glaciers in those regions are considerably larger and lie at higher elevations.

Recent findings suggest that over those 20 years, about 1.5 trillion tons (1,362 billion metric tons) were lost by lake-ending glaciers. This amounts to roughly 28% of all glacier ice lost worldwide.

Studies of single glaciers had disagreed about how much a lake matters. At two glaciers in southeastern Tibet, the loss was dominated at certain stages by ice breaking off into a lake.

Studies in the western Himalaya and British Columbia suggested that lakes played a secondary role.

To weigh the causes, machine learning was used. Here, a program learns which measurements best predict an outcome. Three such programs analyzed the lake-ending glaciers.

For each glacier, the lake’s size and growth were recorded together with 20 years of temperature and precipitation data. Slope, elevation, and latitude were also included.

According to recent reports, of the ice loss the best program could explain, 46% was attributed to a glacier’s shape and position. Climate was assigned 43% and lakes 11%.

Each share carries an uncertainty of 7 to 10 percentage points.

Sources indicate that steeper and higher glaciers tended to lose less ice. Glaciers whose lakes grew more tended to lose more.

Sources indicate that the lakes’ share was highest in regions where lakes had expanded substantially. It was about 14% to 15% in Scandinavia, Alaska, and the southern Andes, and 5% in northern Arctic Canada.

Bolch ranked the causes the same way, placing climate and terrain ahead of lakes, which “significantly exacerbate” the loss.

It has been revealed that deeper lake water pushes up harder on the front of a glacier, which helps floating ice detach. Lake water also melts ice below the surface.

A glacier’s loss is measured by satellites that track the height of its surface. Ice lost underwater can’t be seen that way.

That uncounted loss was estimated at about 62 billion tons (56 billion metric tons) for 2000 to 2020. If it were counted, the total for lake-ending glaciers would be raised by roughly 4%.

With other volume estimates, that figure reaches as much as 8%.

Water that would otherwise reach the ocean is also held back by lakes. Between 2000 and 2023, melting glaciers added about 0.7 inches (18 millimeters) to global sea level.

By comparison, only a small amount was stored in glacial lakes from 2000 to 2020. The team calculated it as about one hundredth of an inch (0.24 millimeters) of sea level. That estimate assumes all the water in the lakes came from glaciers.

The results should make forecasts of glacier change more accurate, Bolch noted.

According to recent reports, mountain regions and the lowlands below them have the most use for such forecasts, Bolch added. A significant share of their water comes from meltwater.

In a recent development, the best program accounted for a little more than half of the differences in ice loss among glaciers. Several of its lake measurements were stand-ins.

Depth matters most right where water meets ice, and direct measurements there are scarce. The team therefore relied on an average depth, which was estimated from each lake’s surface area.

The length of ice touching water came from a single date. The warmth of each lake could only be approximated, using air temperature and lake volume.

Ice thickness at the glacier front wasn’t in the analysis, the authors wrote. Neither was the shape of the ground beneath it.

Anyone assessing the danger of outburst floods from glacial lakes can use the findings too, Bolch said.

In a recent development, future research could measure water depth and temperature at glacier fronts. How the line where ice meets water shifts over time could also be tracked.

In a recent development, physical models built for lake-ending glaciers would give a more accurate answer than statistics, the authors wrote. Such models already exist for glaciers that end in the sea.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Climate Change.

#157343. Physicists have found half the answer to why some materials carry electricity with no loss

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1084 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Physicists have found half the answer to why some materials carry electricity with no loss

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In one copper oxide, flickering electron spins drive high-temperature superconductors, and coupling strength sets where resistance ends.
  • Recent findings suggest that every wire wastes a little of the electricity that runs through it, which is why a phone charger gets warm.
  • A family of copper-oxide ceramics become superconductors at temperatures well above the rest, and physicists have argued for decades about why.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In one copper oxide, flickering electron spins drive high-temperature superconductors, and coupling strength sets where resistance ends.

Recent findings suggest that every wire wastes a little of the electricity that runs through it, which is why a phone charger gets warm. Cool certain materials far enough and that waste disappears.

A family of copper-oxide ceramics become superconductors at temperatures well above the rest, and physicists have argued for decades about why.

For one branch of that family, a team has now matched the strength of one interaction to the temperature at which the loss vanishes.

Electrons in these materials scatter off rapid flickers in the magnetism of the surrounding atoms. The stronger that scattering, the higher the temperature at which the material stops wasting energy.

So, the authors concluded, those magnetic flickers are what pair the electrons up.

Sources indicate that that covers only half of the superconductor family, and the half with the highest temperatures behaves differently. So the answer isn’t complete, and the authors noted so.

Nigel Hussey, a professor of physics at the University of Bristol who also holds a post at Radboud University in the Netherlands, co-led the work. Caitlin Duffy, now a postdoctoral researcher at the French research agency CNRS, ran the experiments.

“Through measurements carried out at the European Magnetic Field Laboratory in the Netherlands and subsequent careful analysis, we have found the smoking gun which solves part of the equation and explains what causes this perplexing state,” Hussey remarked.

Recent findings suggest that in a normal metal, electrons bump into vibrating atoms as they travel, and each collision wastes a little energy as heat. In the oldest known superconductors, those same vibrations do something else at very low temperatures.

They nudge electrons into pairs, and paired electrons flow without resistance.

Industry observers note that that theory has a useful feature. The strength of the pull between vibrations and electrons shows up in a metal’s resistance above the transition, and the same strength sets the transition temperature. Measure one and you can predict the other.

Sources indicate that the copper-oxide materials become superconductors at much higher temperatures, too high for vibrating atoms to explain. Physicists call that temperature Tc.

The leading candidate for a replacement glue has long been the electrons’ own spins, which act like tiny magnets and flicker in step with their neighbors.

What was missing was a measurement tying the strength of that flickering to Tc, the way resistance ties vibrations to it in ordinary metals.

Collaborators at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing grew a thin film of lanthanum cerium copper oxide, one atomic layer at a time.

According to recent reports, along the film, the cerium content changed smoothly from one end to the other. Cerium adds electrons to the material, and the amount sets Tc.

At one end, the film became superconducting at about 25 kelvin, or roughly -415°F (-248°C), which is close to the best this material can do.

Sources indicate that at the other end it never did. Between those ends sat 19 distinct compositions, measured across two films grown the same way, so the amount of disorder stayed the same from end to end.

The team patterned electrical contacts along the film and measured its resistance at each position while varying the temperature and the magnetic field.

The field came from a 35-tesla magnet at the High Field Magnet Laboratory in Nijmegen. This is far stronger than the magnet inside a hospital MRI scanner.

Industry observers note that A magnetic field bends the paths of electrons. How much the resistance rises in a field depends on how often the electrons scatter and from where.

In these films, the pattern pointed to scattering concentrated at particular spots, and those spots matched the ones where electrons meet the flickering spins of neighboring atoms.

According to recent reports, the team then fit the resistance and the field response at all 13 measured positions on one film. Only one number was allowed to change from position to position – the strength of that scattering.

Across the film, as Tc fell from 25 kelvin to zero, that number fell tenfold. Duffy said the field measurements were what made the identification possible.

“Employing some analytical tricks on the data obtained in high magnetic fields, we were then able to identify the dominant source of resistance in this material as scattering off the fluctuating spins,” mentioned Duffy.

“The correlation between the strength of this interaction and Tc then confirmed that the origin for superconductivity in this material is indeed the interaction between the conduction electrons and spin fluctuations,” she added.

One consequence cuts against an earlier idea. Some physicists had argued that the resistance in these superconductors sits at a universal quantum limit.

The scattering strength here varied by a factor of ten across the film, so in this branch of the family, at least, it does not.

Sources indicate that copper-oxide superconductors come in two kinds. Adding electrons, as cerium does here, makes one kind. Removing electrons, which physicists call adding holes, makes the other. The hole-doped materials reach the highest transition temperatures of all.

A tempting guess is that hole-doped materials simply couple more strongly to the same magnetic flickers. However, the team’s earlier high-field measurements on those materials say otherwise.

Industry observers note that in the state physicists call a strange metal, their resistance responds to a magnetic field in a way the same model can’t reproduce. No standard picture of electrons as individual particles has yet accounted for it.

“Although electron- and hole-doped cuprates are made from the same cloth, they are stitched together in different patterns,” Hussey explained.

The result rests on one material, measured on two films, and on a model in which electrons still behave as particles with definite paths. The model’s success here is itself evidence, the authors wrote, because the same approach fails on the hole-doped side.

“While we have found the first key ingredient, the task now is to go and find the second,” Hussey remarked.

It has been revealed that what the second ingredient is, nobody has measured. Finding it, the authors wrote, may take an approach that goes beyond the standard theory of superconductivity, or beyond treating electrons as individual particles at all.

The hole-doped materials are where that search has to happen.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Physics.

#157342. Latest Update: The 7 Best Robot Vacuums Withstood Every Mess We Threw at Them

📅 18 Jun 2020 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3706 w)

It has been revealed that if you find cleaning your house to be a drag, robot vacuums do some of the dirty work for you. These intuitive little machines keep your floors tidy by vacuuming up dust, food crumbs, pet hair, and more—all without requiring you to lift a finger. They’re the ultimate “set it and forget it” cleaning solution because with robot vacuums, there’s no longer a need for you to lug around a heavy canister or upright vacuum.

It has been revealed that robot vacuums have come a long way in recent years. Today’s models are smarter, faster, and more capable than ever before. Many have the ability to map your home’s layout, create custom cleaning routines, and empty their own dustbins.

It has been revealed that they’re also packed with sophisticated sensors to avoid stairs and furniture, dodge socks and dog toys, and skirt past other obstacles. Some models also include mopping functionality for complete floor care. And app and voice control allow you to start, stop, and schedule your vacuum to run from anywhere.

Below, we’ve gathered some valuable tips on what to look for in a robot vacuum and how to use these devices. Plus, find out how we tested the top robot vacuums and which one is best for you.

For models that we tested in-house, we set up three 8-by-8-foot pens, each with a different floor surface, to simulate various cleaning scenarios for each robot vacuum. One pen featured low- to medium-pile carpet. The second had bare, polished concrete, and the third had laminate flooring. We set a stool, floor mat, and ottoman on the concrete to act as common obstacles found in the home.

In each pen, we also scattered flour, dried rice, and crushed up cereal to represent different types of dirt and detritus. This stress test pushed the vacuums beyond typical maintenance cleaning, so we could assess how they handle more material compared to an average encounter.

To better understand how these robot vacuums functioned in everyday environments, we sent several models home with staff members and testers for real-world experience. This allowed us to confidently evaluate how each device handled household challenges like pet hair, kids’ messes, and varying floor types.

Our testers used the vacuums for a month or more, assessing them based on key criteria like features, cleaning effectiveness, navigation capability, ease of use, and overall value. Although these selections were not subjected to standardized lab testing, our recommendations are grounded in hands-on experience and long-term use.

We are continuously refining this list to reflect the latest advancements in robot technology. Our ongoing updates show our commitment to providing trustworthy, up-to-date guidance and selections that are relevant. As new components are introduced and we test more models, we always carefully evaluate and incorporate these insights to help you choose the right tools for maintaining a clean and comfortable home.

It has been revealed that we’ll soon be testing the Roborock QV 35A Robot Vacuum, which is an uprgraded version of our previous Best Overall recommendation, the Qrevo S. The latest model offers much of the same functionality, along with a few improvements—and a couple trade-offs.

Like its predecessor, the QV 35A is a dual system that both vacuums and mops, but it increases suction power up to 8,000 Pascals—1,000 more than the Qrevo S—for stronger cleaning performance. The spinning mop heads reach 200 rotations per minute and lift 10 millimeters, helping prevent carpets and area rugs from getting wet as the robot vacuum moves between thresholds. However, unlike the Qrevo S, the mop heads rely on air drying rather than using a hot air drying system, which could mean longer downtime between cleaning sessions.

According to recent reports, beyond cleaning performance, the QV 35A uses LiDAR navigation to scan and mop your home, creating detailed layouts within the companion app. It stores up to four floor intends, making it a practical option for multi-story households. The app also supports a range of customization features like scheduled cleanings, custom routes. and real-time machine monitoring.

Recent findings suggest that to support all of this, the highly capable docking station is designed for lower maintenance. It holds 2.7 liters of dry debris and 4 liters of water, allowing for several weeks of use before needing attention. Taken all together, these features suggest the QV 35A should perform similarly to the Qrevo S, which handled laminate, concrete, and medium-pile carpet effectively during our previous testing.

Full Roborock QV 35A Robot Vacuum Review.

It has been revealed that if you–or your pet–tend to shed a lot of hair, the Eureka J15 Pro robot vacuum should be your next home cleaning investment. The base has a built-in, automatic hair cutting tool that slices through tangles any time it docks, so you don’t have manually remove hair from the roller.

This robot vacuum isn’t lacking in power, either. It delivers 16,000 Pa suction for a deeper clean, and it works on a variety of floor types like carpet, area rugs, hardwood, linoleum, and tile. The J15 Pro has advanced obstacle detection, and our tester, who has been using this model for months, tells us that it’s great at avoiding furniture, cords, pet toys, and over-friendly pets. It even takes a picture whenever it runs into something in its cleaning path, and you’re able to view the photo within the map afterwards in case it’s something that should be moved liked shoes and cords (or an animal).

The mopping feature is also effective at keeping your house clean. There are two microfiber pads that are spring-loaded to add pressure for a deeper clean, and they extend to get close to walls, corners, and baseboards. Our tester found the J15 Pro to be quiet on all modes, but Turbo is noticeably louder than the nighttime mode. You have control over suction power, though, so it doesn’t have to be running at full capacity constantly if you want to cut down on background noise.

She does mention that while this is a smart device and the app is advanced, it’s a little overwhelming to deal with. There are a plethora of settings and options available, and while it’s easy to set up basic settings initially, it gets a lot more involved. Those who are really just looking for daily maintenance and don’t want all the bells and whistles may find this cumbersome.

Full Eureka J15 Pro Robot Vacuum Review.

As a first-time robot vacuum owner, our tester has been very pleased with his ongoing experience using the dreame X40 Ultra. It’s been able to take on dirt, dust, crumbs, and anything that his dog tracks inside, and exceeded expectations on hardwood floors. There are a few places it struggled to reach, like under a coffee table and TV stand, but we chalk that up to a height problem rather than capability concerns.

Sources indicate that the X40 Ultra has 12,000 Pa of suction power, and a liftable, extendable side brush that gets close to wall corners and furniture legs. To protect rugs and carpets from getting wet, the robot vacuum either detaches the mop heads or lifts them to 10.5 millimeters, preventing any wet and dry mess combinations.

The app also allows you to program no-go zones, including rugs or other problem areas like staircases. Even with pet toys laying around the house, the X40 was able to navigate and map the layout with ease, all while avoiding these obstacles.

According to recent reports, the mopping feature is a favorite for our tester. If you’re constantly on the go, having a robot vacuum capable of mopping on a daily basis is a real game changer. And thanks to auto-empty and auto-refill tanks, it’s really a set-it-and-forget-it device. We only suggest that you run the robot vacuum overnight so you aren’t disturbed by its run cycle. (Waking up to beautiful, clean floors is fun, too.).

Full Dreame X40 Ultra Robotic Vacuum Review.

Ecovacs has been around since the late 90’s, and the brand introduced its first Deebot in 2007. Needless to say, its designs have come along way, and one of the latest versions piqued our interest for one main reason: stain removal.

Industry observers note that most often, robot vacuums with mopping capability can only handle fresh spills on hardwood and tile, not the stubborn, dried-on stuff. The Deebot X12 is trying to change that. It uses an AI camera and infrared stain detector to identify spills, splatters, and even muddy paw prints. Then, it deploys two jets with cleaning solution at up to 46,000 Pascals to loosen residue for the mop roller head to pick up. This could potentially save you from having to make a more detailed pass by hand.

The vacuum has capable power on carpet, too. It uses 22,000 Pascals of suction power to get rid or dirt, hair, and debris, and features an anti-tangle side and main brush to prevent hair from getting trapped around the bristles and roller.

The docking station is one of the more advanced designs we’ve seen in a robot vacuum. It has a bagless dustbin, power washing for the mop roller, and hot air drying. We’re looking forward to testing out this model and updating this guide accordingly with our findings.

Full Ecovacs Deebot X12 Omnicycle Robot Vacuum and Mop Review.

Industry observers note that the Qrevo CurvX is a newer design from Roborock, and we like that is has a slimmer build to fit under a wider variety of furniture, but still packs 22,000 Pa of suction power (the highest on our list). It’s equipped with a range of smart features, including pet recognition technology and two-way video calling (in the Roborock app) to interact with furry friends while you’re away, making it a great choice for households with animals.

The initial mapping process took a bit of time, but alas, this is a crucial step for an accurate layout of your home. Once the mapping was complete, the CurvX navigated efficiently, avoiding unnecessary paths and cleaning strategically as it went. During operation, the vacuum ran very quietly, especially when compared to other Roborock models we’ve experienced.

One of the biggest conveniences is the automatic dustbin emptying system, as it significantly reduces the need for manual maintenance. The tanks hold debris for up to seven weeks, and the water tank automatically refills the reservoir on the robot vacuum so you don’t have to.

It has been revealed that the mop lifting and carpet detection performed well in our lab tests. When used in the concrete floor pen with obstacles like a small rug, it raised the heads with ease when transitioning between floor types. This ensured that carpets didn’t get wet during mopping sessions and the robot maintained the right cleaning mode. The edge mopping system is also a fantastic feature. The mop heads sit on arms that extend outwards for better reach, and they were able to get under and around table legs more efficiently.

That being said, this model isn’t without its limitations. In some of our mess tests, it missed detritus that was close to the pen walls, or “room edges,” despite the side brush kicking up the debris. It got closer than other robot vacuums we tested, but this is still a common struggle for many other models.

Full Roborock Qrevo CruvX Robot Vacuum and Mop Review.

If you don’t need a robot vacuum with mopping capability, then the Shark PowerDetect is a viable option. It doesn’t sacrifice on features where you need them, and works well on different types of flooring.

Industry observers note that our tester found that the robot vacuum could clean various floor types and pick up after pets with ease. After after just one cycle, they noticed the difference.

The vacuum has one side brush, but since it rotates 360-degrees, it’s able to get close to baseboards and edges without leaving much of anything behind. The PowerDetect also does a great job of moving around obstacles. During testing, the vacuum got pretty close to a hair dryer cord to clean as much of the floor/carpet as possible, but it never tried to vacuum over it or got tangled.

Industry observers note that battery life held up too, and the robot vacuum was able to clean multiple rooms before returning to the docking station to charge. Our tester did note that the battery drains faster in Matrix Clean mode, but this isn’t completely unexpected because max suction requires more power.

One of the first things that sets the Eufy Omni S2 is its unique docking station. Most robot vacuums on the market have tanks that are side by side and sit lower to the ground, but the S2’s docking station is taller and more narrow, making it easier to access to refill and empty (and find a place to store).

Another is suction power. The Omni S2 pulls at up to 30,000 Pa, and our tester noticed the difference immediately, especially in high-traffic spots that get flattened and dull over time. The 100 air watts of consistent airflow was able to pull in dirt, allergens, and pet hair from deep between carpet fibers instead of just picking up debris from the surface.

The S2 uses a DuoSpiral main brush, which is actually two separate brush rolls with a gap in the middle to funnel hair into the suction port to prevent tangles, and it has proven reliable in a household with six pets.

Sources indicate that most mopping robot vacuums use spinning mop heads to clean your floors, but the Omni S2 uses a rolling mop with electrolyzed water and plenty of downward pressure for an even clean. The main downside is there is no option for mopping-only or vacuum-then-mopping cleaning modes. Many of our other recommendations are able to do these processes separately, so it’s definitely something to consider. The base station takes care of much of the dirty maintenance work, including self-emptying, self-refilling, hot water washing and hot air drying of the mop roller.

Full Eufy Omni S2 Robot Vacuum and Mop Review.

Many robot vacuums overlap in features and capability, and there are newer and better models releasing all the time. As a result, we’re often adding and swapping out our recommendations in this list. Here are a few other robot vacuums we’ve tested that still warrant recognition:.

Recent findings suggest that eufy X10 Pro Omni Robot Vacuum and Mop: This combination robot vacuum and mop reduces monotonous upkeep tasks with carefully curated features. The docking station lasts for up to 60 days before needing attention, and other key highlights include auto-refill, auto-wash, self-dry, and self-emptying to make maintenance virtually hands-free.

It has been revealed that roborock Curv Flow 2 Robot Vacuum and Mop: The Roborock CurvX we recommend above is the stronger all-around robot vacuum, but the Curv Flow 2 is a good alternative if you want a mop roller that continuously refreshes itself with clean water to prevent dirty mop drag. This robot vacuum is also rated for up to 20,000Pa of suction power, has a larger dustbin, and performs well on hard floors.

Navigation is key to how well a robot vacuum performs its job. Suction matters little if the vacuum fails to cover every part of your floor. Just about all models utilize three fundamental types of sensors to help them navigate.

Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR).

Industry observers note that this navigation method involves a laser that locates features by sending out pulses of light and measuring how long they take to return. LiDAR is especially useful for creating accurate maps and is the most powerful and most common navigation tool for robot vacuums.

Recent findings suggest that with this navigation style, the vacuum travels in one direction and then changes course when it hits an object. A lot of models are programmed to optimize their paths and make them more efficient. By running into a wall in a couple of places, the robot vac can verify the location of the wall and move parallel to it, turning 180 degrees each time they hit an end wall.

Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM).

Recent findings suggest that this triangulates position by tracking multiple points in a room in successive camera frames. Over time, the vacuum learns and becomes more efficient by relying on points that remain constant and do not change.

Sources indicate that suction power, which indicates how strongly a vacuum pulls in air and debris, is typically listed by the manufacturer in pascals (Pa). The bulk of modern vacuums offer anywhere from 4,000 to 10,000 Pa, but with each new model that comes out, we’re seeing those numbers continue to rise, with some upwards of 20,000 Pa. Just be aware that higher suction impacts a robot vacuum’s battery life and noise levels.

A brand’s claims about suction power may not provide the full picture, either. Manufacturers don’t tell us exactly where or how they’re measuring—they may take measurements at the impeller or without passing the filter, or using the vacuum only in a controlled environment. It’s similar to how automakers disclose horsepower ratings on cars as an engine spec. The transmission, differential, and other components all leech some of that horsepower, so what’s actually available at the rear wheels differs from the number listed in the specs.

A large dustbin and water tank capacity are ideal for big homes or households with pets, since they reduce how often you need to empty or refill. For smaller spaces or light daily cleaning, a more compact unit with a capacity of 2 liters should still get the job done. For models that also mop, a clean and dirty water tank of 4 liters or more combined is sufficient for cleaning larger areas efficiently without constant refilling. The models on our list hold between 2.5 and 5.3 liters of debris.

In a recent development, beyond navigation and suction power, today’s robot vacuums come packed with bells and whistles that elevate them beyond the basic models of the past. Room mapping, self-emptying dustbins, voice assistant compatibility, cleaning schedules, and no-go zones have all become more or less the standard.

Recent findings suggest that the most tech-forward robot vacuums offer AI-powered obstacle recognition that identifies and steers clear of pet waste, shoes, or cables. There are also variations that have dual functionality, combining both vacuum and mopping qualities. As you might expect, the more advanced sensors and assets a robot vacuum offers, the higher its price tag.

According to recent reports, throughout our testing process, we discovered that while the mopping features are certainly useful, they don’t fully deliver the type of power or pressure needed to get rid of tough stains or set-in messes. The docking stations are also made for water only, and it’s not recommended to use any kind of detergents or DIY solutions in the robot. Some brands make their own cleaners that you can purchase separately, but make sure its compatible with your specific model. If you’re dealing with really stubborn grime, we recommend keeping a standard mop on hand.

Look out for shoelaces, string, carpet fringe, and thin or lightweight clothing—all of which gets easily caught in brushes and rollers. Some units have sensors that stop them when the brushes meet resistance, and some move in reverse, spitting out whatever they pulled in. This technology isn’t foolproof, so it’s best to just keep the area clear.

Additionally, be aware of pet bowls, plant stands, or other things that could tip over until you know how the robot vacuum interacts with them. Models that leverage bump-and-go navigation may knock things a little harder, so it’s a good idea to set up boundaries to avoid those obstacles.

Lastly, if you have kids, many robot vacuums are capable of picking up small toys (or parts of toys) that are strewn about. A lot of units have the ability to create exclusion zones, so make use of them, or employ your own strategy to avoid all these little hazards that could jam up the vacuum.

Most homes have places where a robot won’t reach, like in between narrowly spaced furniture legs or tight corners. Also, some types of dirt and debris overwhelm robot vacuum filters, since their capacities are pretty small. Fine dust, fireplace ash, and powders, even in moderate quantities, could clog a filter and affect performance.

When set on a consistent schedule, robot vacuums help your house look clean on a day-to-day basis. Still, it’s best to run your upright or cordless stick vacuum for deeper cleans and bigger messes.

Place the robot vacuum and docking station in an open space that’s close to a power outlet. The power connection is essential for charging the vacuum and running automatic dustbin emptying features. When the space in front of the docking station is open and obstacle-free, the vacuum is able to tackle dirt more frequently. Try to avoid putting the unit near high-pile carpeting, near stairs, or cluttered spaces.

For homes with high foot traffic, pets, or children, running your vacuum on a daily basis is ideal. Three to four times a week is best for homes with moderate foot traffic, and if you live in an apartment, or your home has multiple spare rooms that don’t get used very often, running your robot vacuum weekly (or simply as needed) will suffice.

Most units have physical controls on the vacuum to start, stop, and send the vacuum back to the docking station. However, smart features like app control, scheduling, mapping, and voice assistants require internet connection. We recommend connecting the vacuum to your home network to get the most out of these features.
