Industry News: What you just touched can change how the next thing feels

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study in rats found that frontal brain activity helped predict how an earlier vibration would bias judgments about the next one.
  • Industry observers note that what you feel right now depends partly on what you felt a moment ago.
  • A region of the frontal cortex represented both the current and previous vibrations, and its activity helped predict how the previous vibration biased the rats’ judgments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study in rats found that frontal brain activity helped predict how an earlier vibration would bias judgments about the next one.

Industry observers note that what you feel right now depends partly on what you felt a moment ago. In rats trained to judge vibrations, the primary sensory cortex mainly tracked the current vibration.

A region of the frontal cortex represented both the current and previous vibrations, and its activity helped predict how the previous vibration biased the rats’ judgments.

The study was carried out by neuroscientists at SISSA, the International School for Advanced Studies in Trieste, Italy.

“Perception is often thought of as a direct mapping of the external world,” explained Mathew Diamond, a cognitive neuroscientist at SISSA.

“Yet what we experience depends not only on what is happening now, but also on what happened moments ago. In short, every percept is constructed against a backdrop of recent experience.”.

In a recent development, scientists call this effect serial dependence, and it’s easy to picture. “Imagine feeling a vibration with your fingertip (for instance, from the cell phone) and then feeling a second vibration shortly afterward,” Diamond mentioned.

“The second stimulus will not be experienced as an independent event; instead, perception is systematically biased by prior inputs. The brain, in effect, carries traces of the recent past into the present.”.

In a recent development, “Perception is not a photograph of the world. It is more like a film, in which the experience of each frame is influenced by those that came before.”.

Psychologists have known about the effect for a long time. Where the brain does the mixing, and how, has been much harder to work out.

Theories of “predictive processing” propose that the brain constantly combines incoming signals with expectations built from experience. What nobody had clearly shown was the neural machinery that brings the two together.

Industry observers note that to find it, Diamond’s team trained rodents on a simple touch task. On each trial the animal felt a stimulus and had to decide whether it was weak or strong.

Meanwhile, the researchers recorded the activity of hundreds of neurons.

According to recent reports, the animals’ judgments were consistently pulled by the previous trial. After a strong stimulus, the next one was more likely to be judged weak.

It has been revealed that after a weak one, the next was more likely to be judged strong. A medium-strength touch could feel faint or firm depending on what had come right before it.

“The key finding emerged from comparing two cortical regions,” noted lead author Iacopo Hachen.

“Activity in the primary sensory cortex mainly reflected the stimulus right now being processed, a direct representation of the ongoing input.”.

“By contrast, neurons in a frontal cortical area carried information about both the current stimulus and recent sensory history. There, neural representations of the present were embedded within a context established by the past.”.

The first stop for touch signals in the cortex, in other words, stayed true to the present. The frontal region carried the present and the recent past together.

The frontal region also helped predict the animals’ choices.

When its activity rose or fell from one trial to the next, the animals’ judgments shifted in step.

“Variations in this frontal-cortex activity predicted corresponding variations in perceptual judgments from one trial to the next, suggesting that while the sensory cortex faithfully reports the ongoing input, the frontal cortex integrates that input with recent experience to shape perception,” Hachen explained.

One region reports what is happening, and the other decides what it means given what just happened.

The researchers also identified a possible mechanism at the level of individual cells.

Fast-spiking neurons played a prominent role in how the frontal region represented both vibrations. Their firing patterns suggest they may be inhibitory neurons.

There was also an unexpected finding. While a touch was happening, the frontal neurons encoded it as an ongoing sensory event.

Once the animal committed to its answer, the code switched to a different, memory-like format. That stored version lasted and went on to bias the next decision.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, the brain doesn’t just keep a recording of what happened. It rewrites the experience into a new format as it moves from perception into memory.

That rewritten trace then colors the next moment.

The authors see the work as evidence for a basic principle of how the brain works. Perception comes from a constant back-and-forth between fresh sensory evidence and traces of the recent past.

Industry observers note that “Our findings suggest that the brain does not treat each moment in isolation. Instead, the recent past becomes part of the neural representation of the present, a unitary construct that mirrors our experience,” Hachen concluded.

Understanding this exchange could help explain how prediction normally supports behavior, and how it might go wrong in neurological and psychiatric disorders.

The study is published in the journal Science Advances.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1188 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Your home may be full of wildlife you’ve never noticed

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A survey of indoor spaces across the U.S.
  • Homes across the United States and Canada are full of wildlife.
  • A continent-wide survey has found nearly 2,100 species of wild organisms living indoors, mostly insects and spiders, plus centipedes, snails, fungi, and many animals most people have never heard of.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A survey of indoor spaces across the U.S. and Canada recorded nearly 2,100 species, from familiar house spiders to an alligator in a garage.

Homes across the United States and Canada are full of wildlife.

A continent-wide survey has found nearly 2,100 species of wild organisms living indoors, mostly insects and spiders, plus centipedes, snails, fungi, and many animals most people have never heard of.

One record is an alligator that turned up in somebody’s garage.

Sources indicate that this is the largest study of indoor wildlife so far. Nearly all of it is built from photos taken by ordinary people.

The study was led by researchers at North Carolina State University and Colorado State University.

Over 60 co-authors contributed, including museum curators, university entomologists, and independent experts from across North America and Europe.

Ecologists have spent decades cataloging life in rainforest canopies and on the deep sea floor. The places where most of us spend most of our time have received far less attention.

“While researchers have focused significant attention on a variety of natural ecosystems – from rainforest canopies to the deep sea – we know remarkably little about the ecosystems of manmade, indoor environments,” remarked lead author Bradley Allf from Colorado State.

“Our goal with this work was to treat the indoors, at the continental scale, as an ecosystem that we wanted to explore as ecologists,” he explained.

Earlier surveys of indoor life either covered much smaller areas or relied on DNA traces, which can’t always pin down exactly which species was present.

This is the first survey of indoor life spanning the United States and Canada.

The team launched a citizen science project called Never Home Alone on iNaturalist, a website where people share photos of the living things they come across.

Participants were asked to photograph wild organisms in their homes, offices, and other indoor spaces. The rule for “wild” was simple: anything that was neither a pet nor a potted plant.

Industry observers note that submissions came from at least five continents. This study focuses on North America.

Industry observers note that about 3,000 people contributed 23,782 observations, from every US state and every Canadian province. Most were taken in homes, but some came from offices, schools, and airports. The records cover almost three decades, from 1996 to 2024.

In a recent development, every observation was checked by specialists. Dozens of experts identified each organism as precisely as they could.

“This work underscores the value of natural history expertise and the ability to identify species, which is a skillset that is less common among biologists than it once was,” Allf remarked.

It has been revealed that about 95% of the observations were arthropods, the group of animals with jointed legs and hard outer skeletons. Insects made up 60% of all records, mostly beetles, flies, moths, wasps and ants, and true bugs.

Recent findings suggest that spiders accounted for 30%. Animals with backbones made up only 4%, most of them reptiles and mammals.

The rest included fungi, plants, earthworms, snails, small crustaceans, and even single-celled organisms.

Eight species were recorded more than 200 times each.

In order, they were the Asian lady beetle, the brown marmorated stink bug, the house centipede, the varied carpet beetle, the long-bodied cellar spider, the triangulate combfoot spider, the bathroom moth fly, and the eastern parson spider.

“The organisms we found ranged from Asian lady beetles – which were the most commonly found species – to an alligator that unexpectedly turned up in one person’s garage,” Allf noted.

“But one of the things that was striking was how common predator species were – including hundreds of different spider species.”.

Half of the top eight are hunters, and some of them do useful work.

“One study participant noted that they view jumping spiders as working animals, because the spiders play an active role in reducing the population of flies and other pests that they don’t want in their home.”.

Senior author Rob Dunn from NC State pointed out that most people share their homes with these animals every day and have no idea what they are.

“Another thing that is striking about this work is that most people could look over a list of the most commonly found species and wouldn’t know what most of those animals even are – and yet they are around us, all the time,” he stated.

“For example, I suspect most people are unfamiliar with comb-footed spiders, but we have more than a thousand observations of this family of spiders.”.

He sees this as a fairly recent loss.

“This is a stark departure from what we would have expected historically, when our ancestors would have been more aware of the living things around them.”.

Industry observers note that “That’s something we lost. And this is a first step toward regaining that understanding.”.

The list has a very long tail. About 52% of the species were recorded indoors just once.

The true total is almost certainly higher than 2,100, because 44% of the observations couldn’t be identified down to species.

In a recent development, the authors also point out the dataset’s limits. Nobody controlled how hard each person looked, so large, eye-catching animals are probably overrepresented.

And not every animal that ends up indoors actually lives there. Some had simply wandered in and become trapped.

The survey also shows how little is known about even the most common indoor animals.

“It could inform future research in many ways,” Dunn stated.

“For example, house centipedes were the third most commonly found animals, and yet I’m not aware of anyone who is studying them. That’s worth exploring.”.

Some of these animals might even turn out to be useful.

Sources indicate that “For example, we now know that camel crickets carry a microbe that can break down paper products. That could be useful. What else might be out there, in our own homes?”.

“Once we know what’s there, we can begin asking additional questions,” Dunn mentioned.

“Why are these organisms there? What are they doing? Are they beneficial?”.

According to recent reports, “But knowing what’s there is the first step. And it’s exciting because these are the animals we’re around all the time, but we just overlook.”.

Recent findings suggest that the scientists want to investigate how the climate outside shapes what turns up inside. They also initiative to figure out which species have actually adapted to life in buildings.

In a recent development, every record has a date and a location, so the dataset can also serve as a baseline for spotting new arrivals or disappearances in the future. The data are free for anyone to use.

The project is still running, and anyone with a phone can contribute.

Industry observers note that “People can still submit observations to Never Home Alone. The more data the project collects, the more insight we’ll have on the unique and growing ecosystem of the great indoors,” Allf concluded.

The study is published in the journal Ecology.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.
  • The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

It has been revealed that “Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Recent findings suggest that before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

Recent findings suggest that the conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

According to recent reports, “This has never been anything against John Thune,” mentioned Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

It has been revealed that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul remarked.

It has been revealed that whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

Industry observers note that “Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they remarked, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno stated, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

Sources indicate that sen. John Kennedy, R-La., remarked on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

Sources indicate that that long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune mentioned he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

Sources indicate that “If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

In a recent development, if you still aren’t sure about whether or not you think it’s worth the purchase, know that there’s a crop of new hot tubs that can ship right to your door and don’t take too long to set up. It has been revealed that for our recommendations, we focused on how these tubs are built, their lineups of features, and what you’re really getting for the price. Here are the ones worth considering, plus what to know before you commit to this significant purchase.

To guide our selections, we leaned on our own experience owning hot tubs and spas, from basic models to custom setups.

Sources indicate that we chose hot tubs that range from just under $1,000 for inflatable models to high-end models that nearly mimic showroom-quality tubs. But all are available to buy online. Beyond price, we looked at features, capabilities, and fun extras like speakers and ice buckets. Some are a must, while others are mere perks that can elevate your time in the hot tub—and the price.

In a recent development, we pored over customer reviews and expert write-ups. We also consulted Jeff Courter, an engineer and former owner of Cache Valley Spas in Logan, Utah, to get his insights on how you should factor price, setup, and features into your decision.

In a crowded field of plug-and-play spa contenders, the AquaRest DayDream stands out for a long list of relaxing reasons. It’s a legit backyard spa without the headache of professional installation and electrical upgrades, which puts this spa in that sweet spot between bargain shopping and custom installs.

It has been revealed that we like that it plugs into a standard outlet but still delivers a surprisingly strong massage thanks to 35 jets. AquaRest says the DayDream uses a Jacuzzi-branded pump—and while that doesn’t make it a Jacuzzi spa, it’s still a solid indicator you’re getting a reputable, name-brand component under the hood.

There are so many nice extras, like ozone filtration and a lighted waterfall, that make it feel more like a full spa setup than a starter tub. The trade-off is in the materials and power: The roto-molded shell isn’t as luxe as pricier acrylic models, and heating can be slow on 120 volts. It has been revealed that with 170 bubble jets, a multifunction heater, filter, blower, and hard water treatment system, this model has more features than many inflatables. With a capacity of 290 gallons and included headrests, there is plenty of room for lounging. If you like the features of this tub, but have less space to work with, there is also a smaller four-person model available.

In a recent development, we like that—for the price—this hot tub includes a lot of fun extras. In addition to the water treatment and jet specs, there’s also a multicolor LED light system and wireless touch button control panel. There are two headrests, a cover, ground tarp, and storage bag included as well.

In a recent development, we do wish there were more than two headrests for a hot tub advertised for six people, but it’s not a deal breaker. One note: Check your available ground space before ordering, too, as this hot tub has a larger footprint than some other popular models.

This hot tub solves a lot of the complications folks face when seeking a therapeutic experience at home—they may not have the space or ability to upgrade the electrical system.

The hard-sided LifeSmart plugs into a standard outlet, skips complicated installation, and still delivers a solid massage with 13 jets, all in a compact, patio-friendly footprint. If you’re hoping to place this hot tub on an elevated surface, though, it’s important to consult a professional and check the load your deck can bear.

According to recent reports, even compact four-person models like this one can weigh over 3,000 pounds when filled with water, which is more than most standard decks can handle without added support. And while it’s listed as a four-seater, many consumers say it's comfiest with two to three adults.

Industry observers note that if aesthetics matter as much as performance, this Comfort hot tub leans into both. The acrylic shell and clean wood-look cabinet design give it a more built-in, high-end vibe than most entry-level spas (which typically have rotomolded, all-in-one shells). We love the details like LED lighting and water features that make the whole experience feel a bit fancy.

In a recent development, it’s not just about looks, though. With 51 jets and a lounger seat, this tub delivers a more immersive soak than simpler plug-and-play models. The trade-off is in installation. For this model, you’ll need a 240-volt hookup, but that also means those jets will pack a lot of therapeutic power at the end of a long day.

If you want a five-person hot tub that doesn’t require rewiring your backyard, the LifeSmart LS500 keeps things simple. It plugs into a standard outlet, sets up rapidly, and still delivers a comfortable soak with 23 adjustable jets and a lounge seat. We wish there were more, but other features (and price) make up for the lack of bubbles.

Sources indicate that the full-foam insulation and thermal locking cover do a solid job holding heat, which helps keep operating costs in check, and the built-in ozonator cuts down on chemical maintenance. We also like the simple look of this spa, which feels a little high-end for the price bracket. It’s not the most powerful spa in this size range, and heat-up times can be slow, but for an easy, low-hassle setup, it’s a practical upgrade.

Recent findings suggest that while Bestway’s Toronto was our pick for overall best inflatable hot tub, the foam walls do require some extra setup—the process takes two people several hours to complete. On the other hand, the Hot Springs model fully self-inflates in under five minutes and is truly plug-and-play, making it a great choice for those who are purchasing their first hot tub and are not yet familiar with some of the intricacies involved with setting one up and maintaining it.

Everything you need to set it up is included right in the box, with just a level, dry surface and access to an outlet (without an extension cord) required. Despite the lack of foam inserts, this hot tub is still rated for year-round use with Bestway’s Freeze Shield technology. One caveat: While this tub says it's for four to six people, it's really most practical for just four.

The DoCred inflatable hot tub delivers solo relaxation without swallowing up a small patio or using a ton of water. Think of it as an outdoor bathtub, perfect for homes with only showers or those with very limited outdoor space. The oval shape actually makes it easier to fully stretch out compared to some two-to-four-person circular models, and the included side table and mat are a nice touch.

In a recent development, A few drawbacks: Because the heater and bubble jets share the same pump and limited electrical power, activating the bubbles pauses the heating function until the massage cycle ends. That just means you’ll need to make sure the tub is at your desired temp before turning on the jets. This tub also isn’t rated for cold-weather use outdoors, so think of it as a fun addition to your warm-weather outdoor vibe.

Industry observers note that there are two main types of hot tubs: plug-and-play models and hardwired spas. When we reached out to Courter, he recommended considering several factors before making a decision about which type of hot tub you should go for.

In a recent development, “The right choice depends less on preference and more on your setup, budget, and how much installation you’re willing to deal with,” indicates Courter. “There are many things specific to the hot tub being purchased. Things such as whether it is insulated, and what R-value does that insulation have?” R-value measures how well a hot tub’s insulation resists heat loss. The higher the R-value, the better it holds heat, and the less energy it uses to stay warm.

Sources indicate that he notes that some hot tubs run on gas, though for this guide we’ve chosen only electric models. Where you live matters, too. “Ambient temperature will play a big part in operational costs,” he says. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain.”.

Plug-and-play hot tubs are the easiest way in. Most run on a standard 110-volt outlet, so setup is straightforward. They require no electrician, no buried lines, and no major prep beyond a flat surface.

It has been revealed that they’re typically made from molded plastic and are widely available online, which helps keep prices down. There are also some inflatable models on the market for less permanent use.

Industry observers note that the trade-off, however, is performance. These models often have slower heating and less powerful jets compared with higher-end models. Still, for many homes (and especially rentals), this is the most practical option.

Hardwired spas require more planning. These usually run on 240 volts and need professional installation, but they deliver stronger jets, faster heating, and a more refined overall experience.

Most hardwired tubs have acrylic shells and insulated cabinets, which improves durability and efficiency. They also cost more upfront (and installation adds to that), but they feel closer to a traditional showroom spa experience.

It has been revealed that if you’re worried about party-hosting capabilities, be wary. Capacity numbers can be misleading. A “six-person” tub will rarely feel comfortable with six adults. If you have the space, it’s usually worth sizing up.

In a recent development, A four-person model works well for one or two people who want room to stretch out, while six- or seven-person tubs are better for families or hosting. If you’re mainly using it for relaxation or hydrotherapy, a smaller tub is easier to maintain, and often more comfortable day to day.

Sources indicate that take time to think about jet count, but that’s not always a straightforward metric on which to judge a hot tub. What matters just as much is the placement, variety, and adjustability of those jets. Higher-powered pumps will provide stronger flow, as well. A lounger with carefully placed jets is a must if you’re seeking physical relief for aches and pains.

It’s fun to have perks like lights and sound systems, but those matter less than the features that keep a hot tub up and running for years. A good cover in particular makes a major difference. It helps retain heat, reduce energy use, and keep maintenance manageable.

But once you’ve chosen the size and key mechanical specs that meet your needs, it’s okay to jazz up the experience a bit with neat extras like waterfalls and lights. Just be mindful of additional maintenance. It’s easier to buy a new portable Bluetooth speaker than it is to repair one integrated into a hot tub.

Courter remarked that the exact operational cost is hard to guesstimate—a lot of factors come into play. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain,” he indicates. “In Northern Utah, we can get down to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit in the wintertime. In that same timeframe, the average temperature in Miami is going to be in the mid-70s. A hot tub in northern Utah is going to need to run much more often to maintain its temperature.”.

It has been revealed that when it comes to chemicals and cost, that also varies depending on the size of the hot tub and how often you use it. General online user reports vary between $40 and $100 a month, but it’s not a number that’s easy to estimate. The initial setup will cost a bit more as you invest in the chemicals and supplies you’ll regularly need.

Industry observers note that while hot tubs certainly are not a set-it-and-forget-it luxury, they are easier to maintain than a pool—and upkeep should not be a major deterrent. “Maintenance of a hot tub isn’t too bad if you stay on top of it,” claims Courter. “Usually, it takes 10 to 20 minutes once a week to adjust your chemicals and clean your filters.”.

When it comes to chemical options, whether you choose chlorine, bromine, copper, a salt system, or an ozone generator, they all work just fine—as long as you keep your pH in line. “A pH of 7 on the pH scale is neutral, but the pH of a human eye is 7.5, so I always suggest to my customers that they aim for around 7.5,” states Courter.

It has been revealed that other maintenance will involve keeping an eye on the water level, the condition of the hardware, and any signs of malfunction. Some hot tub repairs are simple and you can even DIY them, but many require calling an expert.

Other than structural considerations if you want it on an elevated deck, the options are virtually endless.

Industry observers note that “A factory-built hot tub can go just about anywhere, as long as whatever you are putting it on can hold the weight,” indicates Courter. “A dry hot tub can weigh around 1,000 pounds, but remember that water weighs 8.34 pounds per gallon.” That means an average-sized spa could weigh nearly two tons.

In a recent development, when it comes to ground placement, a flat and level surface with a good base is fine for most uses. If you do choose to place a plug-and-play spa inside your home, be prepared to consult an expert about ways to mitigate moisture damage.

This is another one of those tricky metrics to guesstimate. We’ve listed the warranty windows for each tub we’ve included, but these spas should last longer than that.

“As with most items, it really depends on the quality of the product you buy,” says Courter. He says not all hot tubs are created equal and that consumer research goes a long way. That being noted, spending more doesn’t guarantee a longer life for the hot tub.

“If a customer buys the highest-quality tub on the market and doesn't take care of it, it will fail quickly,” claims Courter. “I have seen many hot tubs fail in just a couple of years if not maintained the way they should. In contrast, my wife and I still use a Watkins Hot Springs that is over 25 years old. Moral of the story: Buy the best quality that you can and take care of it.”.

#157327. Industry News: In a West Texas rock shelter, archaeologists found a hunting kit that was left behind 6,500 years

Industry News: In a West Texas rock shelter, archaeologists found a hunting kit that was left behind 6,500 years

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Archaeologists in Texas uncovered a roughly 6,500-year-old hunting kit with darts, an atlatl and a rare preserved pronghorn hide.
  • Deep inside San Esteban Rockshelter, south of Marfa, Texas, archaeologists recovered parts of a hunter’s weapon kit that someone left behind thousands of years ago.
  • The Center for Significant Bend Studies at Sul Ross State University presented the find in its spring 2025 newsletter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Archaeologists in Texas uncovered a roughly 6,500-year-old hunting kit with darts, an atlatl and a rare preserved pronghorn hide.

Deep inside San Esteban Rockshelter, south of Marfa, Texas, archaeologists recovered parts of a hunter’s weapon kit that someone left behind thousands of years ago.

The Center for Significant Bend Studies at Sul Ross State University presented the find in its spring 2025 newsletter. The center puts the kit’s age at about 6,500 years and calls it “potentially the oldest example of a full weapon system in North America.”.

The kit as a whole has not yet been described in a peer-reviewed study. Only one of its pieces, a spear-thrower known as an atlatl, has been the subject of a journal paper.

The kit includes six stone-tipped dart foreshafts – the front section of a dart – and four self-tipped hardwood dart foreshafts.

There are also four dart nock-ends, the rear tips that fit against the atlatl. A broken hunting boomerang and a partial atlatl complete the weapons.

Sources indicate that the excavators also found a folded pronghorn hide. It had been tanned, and its hair was still intact.

Spaced holes ran around the hide’s perimeter so it could be tied to a frame, as Plains groups often did.

“We just sat there and stared at it in wonder,” said Bryon Schroeder, then director of the center. Someone had folded the hide and set it on top of a rock, he explained.

“And nobody touched it for 6,000 years,” Schroeder mentioned.

An atlatl is essentially a wooden stick with a handle on one end and a hook or socket on the other. It acts as an extension of the human arm, increasing leverage against the dart, the National Park Service explains.

The San Esteban atlatl is described in a 2023 atlatl paper by Schroeder and Devin Pettigrew, an assistant professor at the center.

A radiocarbon date indicates that the atlatl is more than 6,000 years old. That made it the oldest directly dated atlatl in North America at the time, the authors reported in the Journal of Major Bend Studies.

In a paper published in 2026, Pettigrew and other archaeologists at the center measured how fast modern throwers launch darts.

That research shows that heavier darts, paired with strong and skilled throwers, become lethal to very large animals such as mammoths, the center noted.

It has been revealed that “In most archeological sites in Texas, only things made of stone survive,” notes Texas Beyond History, a project of the University of Texas at Austin. The dry Lower Pecos rock shelters are an exception.

It has been revealed that those shelters have yielded hardwood dart foreshafts and rabbit sticks, as well as bow fragments and arrow foreshafts from the bow-and-arrow era. Complete atlatls are very rare even there.

Unique depositional conditions favored the preservation of the Schöningen wooden spears in Germany. A 2025 dating study placed them at about 200,000 years old.

A mammoth-ivory boomerang from Poland is one of the oldest known in Europe, an Obłazowa Cave analysis concluded. A statistical model built on dated bones from the same layer places it between 42,290 and 39,280 years ago.

“We can use the wood to reconstruct the environment and learn more about the amount of time they spent working on tools,” Schroeder stated.

In a recent development, schroeder’s reading of the scene is that a person came to the back of the cave and sorted through the gear piece by piece. Some parts were judged good and others not, and then the person went on their way.

“But that one small act is going to have profound implications in understanding the environment,” he remarked.

Industry observers note that the shelter sits in Presidio County along Alamito Creek, a tributary of the Rio Grande. A spring-fed rock pool, or tinaja, lies in front of it.

The center has worked there since 2019 with the Odyssey Archaeological Research Fund at the University of Kansas. The partners were looking for traces of the region’s earliest people.

The Odyssey fund was established in 2003 with an endowment from Joseph and Ruth Cramer. Its director is Rolfe Mandel, a distinguished professor of anthropology at the university.

In 2020, the excavators uncovered a hearth-like feature with burned and unburned bird eggshells dated to about 15,200 years ago.

In a recent development, “Though this site was pot-hunted in the past, the many large boulders that spalled from the ceiling preserved pockets of shelter deposits,” the Kansas team’s site summary states. Pot-hunting means digging for artifacts to collect.

According to recent reports, the atlatl foreshafts and darts came from intact deposits in an area the excavators call the Sandal Shaft. The Kansas team dates them to about 6,200 years ago, a little younger than the center’s figure.

The pronghorn hide lay about 2 inches (5 centimeters) above them, capped with a metate, a grinding stone.

It has been revealed that the hide yielded a raw radiocarbon age of 5,621 years, plus or minus 24, not yet converted to calendar years. That makes it about 600 years younger than some of the foreshafts and darts, the Kansas researchers report.

The information was obtained from the Center for Big Bend Studies.

Flightless kākāpō parrots from New Zealand are genetically healthy despite 10,000 years of inbreeding

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists sequenced the DNA of Latest Zealand's endangered kākāpō and found that 10,000 years of inbreeding actually helped natural selection clear out harmful genetic mutations.
  • Industry observers note that on Upcoming Zealand’s Stewart Island, flightless parrots called kākāpō spent about 10,000 years cut off from the rest of their species, breeding with relatives.
  • A 2021 study of their DNA found the opposite: the island kākāpō carried fewer harmful mutations than mainland kākāpō, which have since died out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists sequenced the DNA of Latest Zealand's endangered kākāpō and found that 10,000 years of inbreeding actually helped natural selection clear out harmful genetic mutations.

Industry observers note that on Upcoming Zealand’s Stewart Island, flightless parrots called kākāpō spent about 10,000 years cut off from the rest of their species, breeding with relatives. In theory, that should have left the birds with more and more harmful mutations.

A 2021 study of their DNA found the opposite: the island kākāpō carried fewer harmful mutations than mainland kākāpō, which have since died out.

Industry observers note that the researchers wrote that the finding is evidence a small population can survive hundreds of generations of isolation. The species is still critically endangered, though, and many of its eggs fail to hatch.

Industry observers note that nicolas Dussex, a researcher at the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, led the study. Few birds anywhere are as inbred or as endangered as the kākāpō, Dussex said.

It has been revealed that kākāpō likely numbered in the hundreds of thousands before people reached Newly introduced Zealand. Overhunting and predators introduced by people reduced them to 51 birds by 1995.

Fifty came from Stewart Island. The other was a mainland male named Richard Henry.

When the study came out, 201 kākāpō were alive, all on island sanctuaries.

For 49 kākāpō, Dussex’s team analyzed each bird’s complete set of DNA, called its genome. Thirty-five were Stewart Island birds.

The rest were mainland birds: Richard Henry and 13 museum specimens. Those specimens were collected between 1847 and 1924.

According to recent reports, an inbred bird’s DNA has a recognizable pattern. A chick gets one copy of its genome from each parent. When the parents are related, long stretches of the two copies match.

It has been revealed that in the Stewart Island birds, matching stretches made up 53% of the genome on average. In the mainland birds, matching stretches made up 15%.

So the island birds were far more inbred. The team then counted the most damaging kind of mutation, the kind predicted to stop a gene from working.

It has been revealed that mainland birds carried 34.1 of those mutations on average. Island birds carried 17.6 of them, about half as many.

Sources indicate that many of these mutations seem to do harm mainly when a bird inherits the same one from both parents. That happens more often when the parents are related.

It has been revealed that chicks that inherit the mutation from both parents are less likely to survive or breed, the team suggested. Over many generations, the mutation becomes rarer. Geneticists call that process purging.

In a recent development, the team tested the idea with computer simulations spanning 25,000 years. A simulated population that stayed small, like Stewart Island’s, ended up with fewer harmful mutations than a larger one like the mainland’s.

It has been revealed that but in a simulated population one-tenth as large as the island’s, the harm from mutations grew instead. So purging seems to need enough birds for natural selection to work.

After the kākāpō’s recent decline, the team wrote, the birds may now face the same growing harm as that smallest population.

Conservation managers have favored matings with Richard Henry and his offspring, to help the population keep its ability to adapt.

“We show that the single male survivor from the mainland, Richard Henry, has more harmful mutations than Stewart Island birds,” remarked Love Dalén of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, who supervised the study.

“Therefore, there could be a risk that these harmful mutations spread in future generations.”.

In a recent development, richard Henry was also genetically distinct, Dalén added, and may have carried useful genetic diversity. The team recommended weighing that benefit against the risk and, if necessary, limiting breeding between the two family lines.

Sources indicate that dussex’s team counted mutations in DNA and didn’t measure what they do to a living bird. Their effects on survival and breeding weren’t known.

The team called for research into the genetic causes of the kākāpō’s low fertility and hatching success.

Industry observers note that in some other shrinking species, harmful mutations increased as numbers fell, the authors wrote. In others, the mutations decreased.

Next, the team planned to examine other highly inbred birds and mammals, to learn whether the kākāpō is a rare exception.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Genomics.

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

In September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

All that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the New Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

It has been revealed that the heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

Growing mountain ranges played a major role in sparking life on Earth

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rocks once buried in mountain belts suggest Earth's ranges grew taller in two steps, each near a rise in oxygen and in complex life.
  • In a recent development, picture the young Earth and you probably see mountains in your mind.
  • Rocks that were once buried deep inside mountain ranges suggest the ranges grew taller in two steps, a new study finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rocks once buried in mountain belts suggest Earth's ranges grew taller in two steps, each near a rise in oxygen and in complex life.

In a recent development, picture the young Earth and you probably see mountains in your mind. For the planet’s first billion years or more, it may not have had any that would resemble the majestic mountain ranges our planet has today.

Rocks that were once buried deep inside mountain ranges suggest the ranges grew taller in two steps, a new study finds. The first step ended about 2.2 billion years ago and the second about 700 million years ago.

Each step came around the time Earth’s air gained oxygen and life grew more complex.

Matthijs Smit, an associate professor of earth sciences at the University of British Columbia, led the work.

According to recent reports, the link to life is a match in timing, not a demonstrated cause. The authors call it a hypothesis that still has to be tested.

Sources indicate that when two plates collide, rock gets shoved downward as well as up. Minerals that form under that squeeze keep a record of the pressure they felt, and pressure translates into depth.

The deepest-buried rocks that later return to the surface mark roughly how thick a mountain belt’s crust had grown. Smit’s team gathered pressure and age estimates for such rocks from around the world.

The team relied on garnet, a mineral that forms during the burial itself and can be dated precisely. They also added upcoming measurements from ancient rocks in Cameroon and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In an interview with Earth.com, Smit said the debate over the early Earth has run between two pictures.

“Some would argue that it was an almost alien world, with no emerged lands, whereas others would argue that it operated very much in the same way as the modern Earth, with large mountain chains, active tectonics and widespread emerged lands,” he stated.

Before about 2.7 billion years ago, the rocks record burial no deeper than roughly 19 to 22 miles (30 to 35 kilometers). In the long middle era that followed, mountain belts buried rock to 34 to 37 miles (55 to 60 kilometers).

The middle-era depth is roughly double the earlier one. In the current era, rocks have come back from about 56 miles (90 kilometers) down, about half again as deep.

The modern figure matches the crust under the Himalaya and Pamir today.

What surprised Smit was how steady the maximum depth stayed within each era, and how consistently it changed from one era to the next.

“There does seem to be a specific tectonic style for each episode in the tectonic evolution of the lithosphere, which dictates in a broad sense how thick (and tall) mountains could become,” he said.

In a recent development, thicker crust generally stands higher above sea level. Using the relationship between thickness, density, and elevation seen today, the team converted the depths into rough heights.

Before 3 billion years ago, the highest terrain comes out at sea level, within the error bars. Through the middle era, the highest peaks could have stood about 3.1 miles (5 kilometers) tall, roughly half the height of Everest.

Mountains of that era were real, then, but they were not the giants of today.

Recent findings suggest that for the modern era, the method gives about 5.5 miles (8.8 kilometers). That is the height of Everest, K2, and Kangchenjunga, to within the uncertainty.

The authors note the sea-level comparison holds for recent geological time and probably for the middle era too. In the earliest era, the oceans were larger and the crust denser, so those early heights are rougher guesses.

Most of the sediment that rivers carry to the sea comes from mountains, and the amount depends on erosion above about 1.9 miles (3 kilometers) of altitude.

Taller mountains mean more rock washed into the oceans, and with it phosphorus, which limits how much marine life can grow.

In a recent development, both growth periods line up, broadly, with the two great rises in atmospheric oxygen. Each oxygen rise was followed by a Snowball Earth ice age and then by a jump in the amount and variety of life.

Recent findings suggest that strontium in ancient seawater, which tracks how much material was coming off the continents, also rose during both periods. Phosphorus would have behaved the same way, the authors argue, because it is held in similar minerals.

“It’s likely not a coincidence that life on Earth developed and diversified approximately during the same period that the two growth spurts occurred,” said co-author Ellen Kooijman of the Swedish Museum of Natural History.

The match isn’t perfect, and the authors say so. Some records of oxygen and living matter don’t move in step with the mountains. That could mean the hypothesis is wrong, or that the planet responded to extra nutrients in thresholds and delays.

Sources indicate that why would mountains grow taller only at certain times? “We suspect that these increases are ultimately linked to the cooling of our planet,” Smit remarked. “As a result, the process that makes mountains changed, allowing mountains to grow taller.”.

In the authors’ reading, the first change was the arrival of plate tectonics as we know it, with one plate sliding beneath another and crust piling up.

The second came as the cooling mantle let continental margins be dragged deeper before snapping free. That is how the thickest mountain belts are built today.

According to recent reports, old, deeply buried rocks rarely survive. Such rocks are the most likely to be altered by later events or lost back into the mantle, so the record is thinnest exactly where the first step happened.

Smit told Earth.com that the first change is pinned down only to a window of several hundred million years, ending around 2 billion years ago.

“We don’t know precisely how this change occurred in time and whether it was even one continuous change or whether there were short bursts by which mountains were able to get higher and higher,” he said.

Until that window narrows, the timing can’t be checked closely against the changes in the oceans and atmosphere, Smit said.

It has been revealed that that work starts with more field research in ancient terrains, sampling rocks and measuring their pressures and ages. He also suggested Earth system models that include step-like, tectonically driven increases in phosphorus.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances. Co-authors are at Utrecht University, the Swedish Museum of Natural History, and the Geological Survey of Canada, among others.

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that unlike window air conditioners, portable air conditioners roll easily from room to room and take only minutes to set up—no brackets, no tools, no sweating through a complicated installation before you can start sweating less. Most just require a nearby window and wall outlet to get cold air flowing. Yes, they tend to cost a bit more than window units, but the tradeoff is real: you can’t beat the convenience their portability adds, which is why many people choose them over other models. Plus your view isn’t blocked by a giant metal box.

Industry observers note that portable air conditioners have an internal fan that moves hot, humid air over a refrigerant-gas-filled coil to cool and expel it into a room to lower the temperature. The moisture it strips from the air collects in an internal reservoir that you’ll periodically need to drain. Higher-end units either pump it out automatically or evaporate it entirely so you never have to think about it. Because the whole unit rolls on casters, you can take the cold air with you instead of running more energy intensive central a/c or buying multiple window units.

Sources indicate that to find the best models to recommend, we tested air conditioners from trusted brands like LG, GE, Black + Decker, Midea, Hisense, and more. These are the units that stood out and are worth the investment.

Sources indicate that we placed each unit in its own room and directed its discharge hose to the outside, then set the appliance’s temperature to 68 degrees and its fan speed to maximum. We directed the cold air each unit discharged at a target 8 feet away, then used an infrared thermometer to measure the temperature at four different locations on the target. We also checked the appliance’s outlet to see if it maintained a consistent temperature. To test the wheels’ durability and noise, we rolled each unit on a hard surface to maximize squeaks and rattles.

We also sent several air conditioners to our staff’s homes and apartments for further testing, where our editors used them over the course of weeks within the living spaces. We tested how easy they were to use, how they operated over time, and how easy they were to integrate into daily life.

According to recent reports, for our most recent revision, we identified the most trusted brands and surveyed current models across a range of price points, BTU capacities, and capabilities, making sure we had options for small rooms and larger ones. From there, we narrowed the field by prioritizing units with strong efficiency ratings, straightforward setup, and drainage designs that won’t require constant attention.

In a recent development, our top-rated portable air conditioner stands out for how quickly it cools down a room. During testing, we turned it on and almost immediately began feeling a cold blast of air with very little runtime. The a/c noticeably brought down the temperature in just a few minutes, plus it did so quietly. According to LG, the unit operates at just 44 decibels on its lowest setting.

Industry observers note that the unit has three modes: cooling, fan, and dry. Cooling and fan are pretty straightforward while dry actually turns the unit into a dehumidifier. So, when you don’t actively need it, feel free to have it run in moist spaces like your laundry room or garage.

Sources indicate that the louvers on the a/c unit can be set to move up and down on their own. This actually made a pretty notable difference in full-room air circulation and helped get rid of hot air that sat near the ceiling.

Setup was also quite easy, as the air conditioner was almost fully assembled right out of the box. Even connecting the hose and slider into the window was intuitive and took less than 5 minutes total. With the four wheels and very basic setup, we were rolling it from room to room in no time.

Full LG Portable Air Conditioner Review.

According to recent reports, if you’re hesitant to spend over $500 on a portable air conditioning unit, this option from Dreo is the best bang for your buck. Considering the relatively low price, its power and added features surprised us during testing.

First and foremost, the unit blasts cold air quite promptly. In fact, it worked nearly as well as several of the more expensive units we tested. The window exhaust has a foam seal to make sure no hot exhaust or exterior air sneaks in.

The air conditioner pairs with Dreo’s app for connection and precise programming, however we ended up using (and loving) the physical remote. It has 10 buttons for changing the speed and temperature, setting the air mode, operating the sleep timer, turning on the auto-swing louver function, and more. Plus, there’s an attached magnet for convent storage on top of the unit.

On the front of the unit there are manual controls and a digital display that demonstrates the room temperature, mode, and fan power. So whether you’re using the remote, app, or changing settings manually, you know exactly what the status is.

This Whynter’s amperage and BTU capacity position it firmly in the heavy-duty cooling category. The same applies to its dehumidifying power, with the unit capturing up to 71 pints of moisture per day. The biggest downside is that it’s also firmly in the heavy category, weighing over 70 pounds.

The portable air conditioner has a dual-hose design (intake and exhaust) for reducing the amount of condensate that the a/c collects, since it’s supposed to be removed in the exhaust air stream.

According to recent reports, A similar model (ARC-14SH) also operates in heat pump/heater mode. For a slightly smaller model, check out the Whynter Elite ARC-122DS below.

Sources indicate that while most units are either quiet or powerful, the GE Profile Portable A/C offers a bit of both worlds. Because of its dual-hose design, the air conditioner takes in air at a much higher rate than one that relies on the body of the unit to do this work. With more air coming in, more cold air comes out. This was definitely true during testing.

On its average setting, the a/c noticeably cooled down a mid-sized room in less than ten minutes. Holding up my hand to the vents, I felt a cold blast of air much stronger than other options I tried out. Going even further, the Profile has a turbo mode that turns the fans up to an even higher level.

Sources indicate that the effectiveness of the cooling has do to with more than just airflow, too. This portable a/c unit also comes with auto louvers that more evenly distribute cold air by shifting the vents up and down. I particularly like this feature for apartments like mine which are a few floors up and end up with a lot of accumulated hot air near the ceiling. The auto louvers help bring down the temperature of the entire room down as opposed to just blasting cold air in one direction.

According to recent reports, while all these features impressed me, the unit’s best quality is that it doesn’t stand out at all. This a/c is incredibly quiet. While I barely noticed the sound at normal levels, when I set the unit to quiet mode, the noise levels drop to a whisper. According to GE, quiet mode is measured at just 42 decibels, which is lower than all other options we recommend.

This makes the Profile an ideal choice for overnight use or in small rooms. However, the remote control buttons don’t light up, so if you’re using it at night, you may need a flashlight, phone, or bedside lamp.

It has been revealed that if the other units on this list take up more real estate than you have or want to give, the Dreo AC319S is the one you won’t have to make room for. It's the most compact refrigerant-based portable air conditioner we've included—at just over 17 inches wide and 28 inches tall, it slips into corners and tight apartments where bulkier units don't fit. Be warned, though, the tradeoff for that smaller footprint is smaller cooling coverage. This one is best for bedrooms, home offices, and other spaces up to 300 square feet.

But what it gives up in cooling-size capabilities, it makes up for in smart features and low maintenance. The drainage-free system, powered by Dreo's patented internal pump and dual water sensors, handles condensation automatically. In moderately humid conditions, you'll likely never need to drain the unit at all. The Dreo app sends a notification if the tank does fill up, which is a thoughtful touch. That kind of hands-off convenience is why this one made our list.

In a recent development, at just 45 decibels on its lowest setting, it's whisper-quiet on par with the priciest units here. Smart controls are also unusually comprehensive. In addition to Alexa and Google Assistant, the AC319S works with Siri, making it one of the only portable ACs that pairs nicely with Apple products. The circular LED display looks sharp, though you can’t dim it, so keep that in mind if you proposal to use it overnight in rooms you want to stay dark.

If you’re fortunate to have a large living room, an open-strategy studio, or a finished basement, you know the luxury of size comes with a cost—cooling oversized areas can be tough. To beat the heat in big rooms, the Whynter ARC-1230WN is the unit we’d point you toward.

Sources indicate that with 14,000 BTUs, it covers up to 600 square feet—more than any other unit on this list. In independent testing, it dropped room temperature by about 12 degrees in a single hour, a result no other unit came close to matching.

A major part of that performance comes from Whynter's hose-in-hose dual-hose design. Unlike a standard dual-hose setup, the intake and exhaust lines run concentrically inside a single tube, preventing heat leakage between the airstreams and improving overall efficiency. The inverter compressor, which ramps up and down rather than cycling on and off, keeps noise down once the room reaches your set temperature and reduces energy use.

Sources indicate that according to Whynter, the inverter technology delivers 20 percent more cooling capacity and over 40 percent energy savings compared to non-inverter models. In a recent development, if you're shopping for a portable AC because you have a room your HVAC system can’t handle, the Midea Duo MAP14HS1TBL is our top recommendation. Sources indicate that the dual-hose design pulls in fresh air and expels exhaust air through a single concentric hose, keeping a neutral pressure balance in rooms. This prevents warm outside air from coming back in through gaps and cracks. Midea's airflow system also projects air up to 26 feet, which makes a real difference in longer rooms where less forceful units only cool the area immediately around them.

We’re also impressed by the smart controls. The SmartHome app works on iOS, Android, and Apple Watch, and voice control is compatible with Alexa and Google Assistant. According to recent reports, we were pleasantly surprised by the power and value offered by this small portable air conditioner from Black+Decker. It begins producing cold air very quickly, though not quite at the volume of many other air conditioners we tested. That said, it still reduced the temperature of its target at a rapid rate.

According to recent reports, the unit provides multiple fan speeds, dedicated dehumidification, a timer setting, and a sleep setting. Note that there is no heater setting on this appliance. It’s meant to cool and dehumidify exclusively.

Sources indicate that reviews Editor Amber Joglar tested out the four-in-one version of this model which also functions as a heater. After just 10 minutes of use in her room, Joglar felt, “a noticeable shift in the air temperature.”.

Sources indicate that the quick cooldown times stood out across both models, though Joglar also pointed out that this led to the exhaust pipes heating up quickly as well. This isn’t necessarily a problem, but if you blueprint on using the unit for several hours a day, consider covering the tubes in insulation.

In addition to the cold air, Joglar liked the remote and LED control panel, saying, “I normally just change settings on the air conditioner itself because it’s right next to my bed, so backlit controls are helpful.”.

Similarly, the remote control is great for when she’s already in bed or wants to pre-cool the room before she’s ready to go to sleep.

Joglar’s model also heats rooms. So, instead of storing it in a closet or attic for the cold winter months, she simply switches functionality.

Read Our Full Black+Decker Portable Air Conditioner Review.

Coverage area is one of the most important factors in choosing an air conditioner. Manufacturers rate units in square footage, but that number assumes an average ceiling height (roughly eight feet) and room insulation. If the room is especially hot in the summer (for example, it’s a finished attic or it has large, south-facing windows) we recommend bumping up to the next size rather than buying a unit that will run constantly and struggle to keep up.

In a recent development, an air conditioner’s cooling capacity is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTU, per hour. To gauge coverage, figure roughly 20 BTU per square foot of space. Most portable a/c units range from 5,000 to 20,000 BTUs, which puts their effective range roughly between 350 and 700 square feet. So when in doubt, size up—an oversized unit cycles off when it hits your target temperature, while an undersized one never stops trying.

Single-hose units essentially recirculate the room’s air to cool it and have one line that runs outdoors to expel exhaust. The catch is that expelling air creates a slight negative pressure in the room, which pulls in warm air from other parts of the house and from outside through gaps around doors and windows. It works, but it’s working against itself.

Dual-hose units solve this by pulling outside air in through one hose for cooling and pushing hot exhaust out through a second hose. The result is a more self-contained system that’s noticeably more efficient, especially in larger spaces. The tradeoff is price.

Industry observers note that because dual-hose models are more complex, they tend to be more expensive. If you only have a small space to cool, a portable a/c with a single hose may suit your needs just fine. For anything larger, the dual-hose design is worth seriously considering.

Hose length determines how far away from a window you can maneuver your portable air conditioner. If you set it up in a large room, or one where the nearest window is far from where most people gather, hose length becomes more important.

It also plays a key role in room setup. If the hose isn’t long enough to set the air conditioner in front of large furniture pieces, you may have to rearrange the room for the most effective cooling. Most hoses range anywhere from 50 to 90 inches fully extended. This should give you enough space to make adjustments and pull the air conditioner closer to the center of the room if needed.

According to recent reports, most portable air conditioners hover between 50 and 60 decibels while they’re running—that’s roughly the noise level of a normal conversation. In most cases, that’s fine during the day, but if you’re planning to run the unit in a bedroom overnight, those numbers start to matter.

Sources indicate that units that dip below 50 decibels in their quietest modes are on par with most ceiling fans and are easier to sleep through; a few on this list get impressively close to whisper-quiet. Pay attention to the decibel rating at the unit’s lowest fan setting, not just its average operating level.

In a recent development, much like larger ductless mini-split air conditioners, some portable air conditioners include a heat pump. “If you’re shopping for an a/c unit because you have a space not currently cooled or heated, one of these models may warrant consideration,” says gear editor Bradley Ford. “Similarly, you may have a room that your HVAC system doesn’t reach effectively. Rooms like this are typically either too cold or hot, depending on the season. If this is the case, a unit with heating capabilities may be able to fill your HVAC gap.”.

Industry observers note that every portable a/c pulls moisture out of the air, similar to home dehumidifiers. The question is what happens to it next. Budget units collect it in an internal pan that you’ll need to manually drain, sometimes daily in humid conditions.

In a recent development, other units use self-evaporating technology to push moisture out through the exhaust hose with no bucket to remember. A few high-end models go even further, offering a continuous drainage port where you can attach a hose and never think about water again. If low-maintenance matters to you, the drainage method is a factor to consider.

Sources indicate that there isn’t a clear superior option between window units and portable options. Choosing between the two largely depends on your home, windows, and personal needs. That said, window air conditioning units are generally faster at bringing temperatures down and run more efficiently than their portable counterparts.

Portable air conditioners have certainly closed the gap over time in terms of cooling ability, but still lag behind if that’s your number one priority.

Portable units stand out because of their convenience and ease of setup. If you don’t have compatible windows, get a portable unit. If you need quick cooling in a spot that generally doesn’t need air conditioning, get a portable unit. If you want just one machine for your entire apartment, get a portable unit.

Portable air conditioners are compatible with a lot more window openings than window units, so you can use them regardless of your apartment or home fixtures.

Industry observers note that new portable a/c units are relatively energy efficient across the board. That noted, it’s certainly a sliding scale. There are several ways in which energy efficiency is calculated for air conditioners, but the shorthand is if your a/c unit is Energy Star-certified, it’s worth getting.

For items that don’t have Energy Star certification, pay attention to the CEER, EER, and SEER numbers. In short, look for an air conditioner with a CEER above 10, with anything above 12 qualifying for Energy Star certification. Similarly, look out for a SEER above 14 in the north and 15 in the south as well as an EER above 10. These are general numbers, but serve as a basic guide when choosing between different options.

One of the biggest issues to solve with portable air conditioners is cooling efficiency. While most units generate a ton of cold air, leakage from the hose or exhaust port can work against that. There are two key things you can do: insulate the opening in the window and insulate the hose itself.

Sources indicate that many portable units provide foam pieces that fit in and around the window insert to minimize the amount of hot air that leaks in from outside. The hose itself won’t come with foam insulation pieces, but you can perform a similar trick by buying one online or by making one yourself. Some people use blankets while others have used everything from reflective sun shades to Amazon plastic packaging. The goal is to prevent heat from the tube from radiating into your living space.
