📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.
  • It has been revealed that last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout.
  • According to recent reports, one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

It has been revealed that last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, Latest England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.).

According to recent reports, one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”.

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

It has been revealed that which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”.

In a recent development, #MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

According to recent reports, republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a latest congressional map.

Recent findings suggest that california contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a latest congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Sources indicate that tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Guv patch: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

In a recent development, senator Morrison? Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

Sources indicate that AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a newly introduced organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is Latest Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Recent findings suggest that congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”.

Ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The Latest York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Recent findings suggest that here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

Sources indicate that how Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

According to recent reports, was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”.

Song of the cycle: The Latest York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The Fresh York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

If those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

#157247. Latest Update: Humans Will Go Backwards in Time Within 3 Years, a Scientist Indicates. But How Would We Know?

Latest Update: Humans Will Go Backwards in Time Within 3 Years, a Scientist Indicates. But How Would We Know?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Getting older usually means having fewer years ahead of you.
  • It has been revealed that the advances are arriving fast enough, he indicates, that every birthday could come with the gift of replacing the year you just lived.
  • Sources indicate that kurzweil calls this “longevity escape velocity.” In a March 2024 interview, he put it even more dramatically, as going “backwards in time.” You’d still technically be getting older, at least by conventional standards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting older usually means having fewer years ahead of you. But futurist Ray Kurzweil thinks modern medicine might be on the cusp of changing that, possibly as soon as 2029.

It has been revealed that the advances are arriving fast enough, he indicates, that every birthday could come with the gift of replacing the year you just lived. After that, he predicts, it’s possible that we’ll all start actually gaining time.

Sources indicate that kurzweil calls this “longevity escape velocity.” In a March 2024 interview, he put it even more dramatically, as going “backwards in time.” You’d still technically be getting older, at least by conventional standards. But your expected remaining years of life would go in the opposite direction, getting longer with each passing year as medical interventions improved.

Industry observers note that our earlier coverage took a closer look at that prediction and Kurzweil’s argument about how accelerating medical advances could get us there. S. Jay Olshansky, a professor emeritus of epidemiology and public health at the University of Illinois Chicago, has a less enthusiastic name for it.

“I refer to LEV as voodoo demography,” he tells Popular Mechanics.

Yet Olshansky thinks research into slowing aging could produce crucial benefits, too. His objection concerns the much bigger promise that those benefits will keep arriving fast enough to outrun aging itself.

Life expectancy describes a population, while lifespan is how long an individual actually lives. To determine life expectancy, researchers calculate how many people die at certain ages and come up with statistical predictions. Plenty of people will live longer, and plenty will die sooner.

That distinction matters when somebody promises to add years to your life. The Social Security Administration’s 2023 period life table, for instance, gives a 60-year-old man 21.79 remaining years and a 61-year-old man 21.04. Both calculations assume that 2023 death rates continue throughout the rest of their lives. They illustrate how expected remaining years generally shrink with age under fixed conditions.

In a recent development, kurzweil’s prediction depends on medicine improving fast enough to beat those numbers, and to keep beating them every year. Imagine a 60-year-old who is expected to live about 22 more years. If treatments got better rapidly enough, that person could turn 61 and find they now had 23 years ahead instead of fewer. That would be an impressive gain. But one year of progress wouldn’t be escape velocity. To stay ahead of aging, medicine would have to do the same thing the next year, and every year after that. Without that continuous progress, it’s just wishful thinking.

It has been revealed that olshansky wants to know what evidence would convince Kurzweil’s supporters that humanity had actually reached escape velocity. Beating one disease wouldn’t be enough. A treatment might save someone from one illness and give them more years, but another illness could still cut that life short.

Industry observers note that olshansky does see reason for hope in aging research. He says work underway “likely will yield reductions in the rate of biological aging.” That could mean people develop age-related illnesses later in life than they would otherwise, giving them more years in good health.

Olshansky would look at whether a treatment changed people’s chances of dying as they got older. Do illnesses show up later, and do people really survive longer? “It’s important that total mortality be the measurable endpoint,” he indicates. A treatment might prevent a heart attack, but that wouldn’t protect a patient from dying later from cancer. Researchers would have to count deaths from all causes to see whether a given treatment actually bought people more time.

It has been revealed that suppose a treatment delayed several illnesses and helped recipients live longer. That could change how people planned their later years, even if medicine never caught up with aging. People could have more good years after they stopped working, and some might choose to stay on the job longer. Before making those plans, people would need to know how much longer the treatment could keep them alive and well.

Recent findings suggest that for now, gains in life expectancy have been getting harder to come by. In a 2024 study in Nature Aging, Olshansky and his colleagues analyzed the death rates between 1990 and 2019 in places where people live the longest, as well as in the United States. Life expectancy was still generally growing, but the pace of that growth had slowed.

Olshansky explains that much of the big rise in life expectancy in the past came from keeping children alive and preventing mothers from dying in childbirth. Saving a child’s life can add decades to a population’s average life expectancy. But in countries where most people already live into their 70s and 80s, those gains have mostly been made. The remaining deaths happen mainly among older people, and saving an 85-year-old from one illness adds far fewer years. That’s why it’s key to slow down aging. If researchers could slow the biological process behind many diseases of old age, life expectancy might start rising faster again. That possibility, Olshansky indicates, is what makes the research worth pursuing.

If only a few people received an anti-aging treatment, the country’s life expectancy wouldn’t change, Olshansky claims. To find out whether the treatment works, researchers would have to follow the people who took it and compare how long they survive with similar people who didn’t.

Industry observers note that and the only way to confirm a promise of 20 extra years is to watch people live them. “A specific prediction of a numerical gain in either life expectancy or lifespan associated with an intervention would require an observed gain of the predicted amount,” he notes. Encouraging early results could justify more research, but they couldn’t show how much time a treatment added. Scientists could have good news in 2029 and still need decades to learn how many years people actually gained.

Even then, one success wouldn’t mean we’d reached escape velocity. Kurzweil’s prediction needs each advance to arrive in time to add more years, then another advance to do the same, and another after that. Kurzweil has stated that people could still die even if medicine delivered the gains he predicts. Olshansky’s worry is that grand promises could overshadow the research he’s most hopeful about: work that could actually slow aging.

Slowing aging alone would give people plenty to look forward to, deadline or not: more years, and the health to enjoy them. Finding out how many years would take patience, because the people in those studies would still be busy living.
